I introduced last year.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO PLACE INLAND MERCHANT SHIPPING UNDER RAILWAY COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO PLACE INLAND MERCHANT SHIPPING UNDER RAILWAY COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is coming to a
time when this Bill is looked upon possibly as a hardy annual, but I hope it is coming to a time when members on both sides of this House will appreciate to the full the importance of the measure and will vote to place it on the statute book. The purport of the Bill is to bring boats on our inland waters under the control of the Railway Commission. I have eliminated an important clause in the former Bill dealing with the question of controlling boats on our coasts. This Bill confines the control entirely to boats on our inland waters, and there is in the Bill a clause defining the limits contained in our statutes regarding inland waters. I do not need to tell members of the House that I hope the Bill will receive their approval, and that it will be placed on the statute books during the present session.

Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 55, to amend the Fertilizer Act, 1909. He said:	It is not proposed by this Bill to make any drastic changes in the Fertilizer Act. This Bill is simply to provide for the better marking of commercial fertilizer which is offered for sale, so that the farmer may know exactly what he is purchasing. It is proposed that the manufacturer of fertilizers shall specify the material from which his different chemicals are derived, also the available phosphoric acid in the contents of his fertilizer. I believe a majority of the fertilizer manufacturers of Canada would be in favour of this amendment, from the very fact that a few unscrupulous manufacturers of fertilizer are putting into their compounds ingredients which are not plant food, such as ground leather, and mustard seeds, which have a large content of ammonia.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

In

That, in the opinion of this House, an indemnity should be paid the innocent victims who during the so-called Quebec riots of 1918 have either been killed or wounded by the soldiers of His Majesty.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it was my privilege last year to place before the House certain facts which, to my mind, should have j'ustified the Government in paying some indemnity to those innocent victims who, during the so-called Quebec riots of 1918, were either wounded or killed by His Majesty's soldiers. At that time we had from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), certain declarations that led us to believe that the Government would institute an inquiry and give these people an opportunity to state fully and fairly their claims in this matter. Unfortunately, notwithstanding these declarations, no action has been taken, and I am compelled, under the circumstances, to put the matter once more before the House in a different form, and to ask hon. members to concur in the opinion that an indemnity should be paid
to these people on whose behalf I now speak. My motion of last year was one for the production of papers. I moved:
For a copy of all reports, letters, petitions or documents referring to claims for damages on behalf of innocent victims who, during the so-called Quebec riots of 1918, have either been killed or wounded by the soldiers of His Majesty?
This motion was accepted by the Government, and on April 29 the Secretary of State produced the following document:
Sessional Paper No. 140: Thursday, April 29, 1920. Return to an Order of the House of Commons, dated April 14, 1920.
Canada, Department of the Secretary of State.
Answers No information.
I was very much surprised at this answer because, to my personal knowledge, letters had been exchanged between certain persons and the Government, between certain persons and the Prime Minister of the day (Sir Robert Borden), and between certain persons and the Minister of Militia. On the strength of this information I communicated again with the parties interested and I received copies of letters which they wrote at the time to the Government. I know of one man particularly, G. Alfred Mercier, who wrote to the Minister of Militia, and the Prime Minister of the time a good many letters, and answers were received from both hon. gentlemen. I mention this fact, in passing, to show that there was no reason why the Secretary of State of that time should state that there was no information on the subject, when as a matter of fact, a number of letters had been exchanged and certain claims made. The only inference, so far as I can see, is that the matter was considered trivial by the Government of that time. To my mind the matter is not one that should have been treated lightly. A number of persons were killed, persons who were innocent victims, and it is not a case for refusing to entertain the claims that are being advanced. The people of that part of Quebec city suffered a grievous wrong. The wound then inflicted is still unclosed and it will so remain unti^ the Government adopts measures of a remedial character and treats fairly those persons who have suffered so grievously.
I do not intend to repeat at any length the remarks which I made last year on this subject; but in order that the House may have a better grasp of the facts it is necessary that I should refer to some of the more important cases to which, at that

time, I called the attention of the Government. I do not intend to condemn the Government for sending troops to Quebec on the occasion in question. A year ago I said, and I now repeat the statement, that the Government were influenced in acting as they did by special circumstances; they were badly advised by the reports of the men who represented the Canadian press at the time of the occurrence and who gave to this small trouble such exaggeration and such publicity that the Government were deceived with respect to it. I have already characterized the occurrence as "a small trouble." In that statement I am supported by the views expressed by the Quebec Chronicle, a paper which supported the Government throughout that period. The editorial in the Chronicle was written the day following the events referred to, and from it I quote the following sentences :
Assuredly it would be foolish and unfair to allege that the natives of St. Roch's as a whole were guilty of acts of anarchy and we specifically state not only that what has taken place has been "the work of an excited populace," but also that only a relatively small minority of irresponsible youths "were involved".
Influenced by the publicity given to this small trouble troops were sent down to Quebec, and, prejudiced as the troops undoubtedly were, it is a wonder that other unfortunate acts did not occur in addition to those which actually happened. Still the actual events were sufficiently serious and greatly to be deplored. First I would draw attention to the case of Lecours. But first let me state that I will not take the responsibility of affirming that what these men say is correct; I will say, however, that I have no reason to believe they are stating anything contrary to the facts. I took the trouble of writing to each of the sufferers to ask him to put in writing what he had to say. I will first read the letter addressed to me by Lecours, which is dated at Buffalo, N.Y., March 22, 1920:
Mr. George Parent, K.C., M.P.,
70 St. Paul Street,
Quebec.
Dear Sir,-On the first of April, 1918, I was the proprietor of a store situated on the Iron Stairs, Crown street, in which I sold cigars candies, cigarettes, etc. About 10.30 p.m., on the 1st of April I thought in view of the fact that the soldiers were guarding Crown street and the Steps, that it would be well to close my store earlier than usual. I had just put up my blinds and locked my door when a party of twenty-five or thirty soldiers suddenly burst the door and entered. Several of them struck me with their rifle butts on the head and elsewhere and threatened me with death. They took away the money which was in the drawer as well as

several boxes of cigars and cigarettes and broke my window panes. I have already sent in my account to the Militia Department which refuses to pay on the grounds that the city is responsible.
Yours very sincerely,
,	A. J. Lecours,
38 Cottage street,
Buffalo, N.Y.
This letter speaks for itself. I shall dispense with comments except to draw attention to the writer's statement that he has "sent in his account to the Militia Department." If this be true, how could the Secretary of State declare on April 29, 1920, that he had no information concerning the claims referred to in the statement presented by me last year? Are we to presume that both gentlemen are right in their respective contentions?
The next case is the one of Joseph Blouin, and it well deserves attention. Here is what Blouin says in a letter addressed to me:
In answer to your letter requesting details of the wounds which I received during the time of the Quebec riots, and asking me whether I was one of the rioters, I may state that I was not. I was travelling on St. Valier street when I was attacked. I was going home at half past five in the afternoon on Sunday the 31st of March, the day before the riots. I was bayoneted four times. These bayonets penetrated the abdomen and moreover I was struck by the butt end of a riffe on the head to such an extent that my health has diminished fifty per cent and according to my physicians I will be obliged to undergo an operation every two years for the rest of my life. I have given full information to Doctors George Racine and Simard, of the Hotel Dieu, and if I should happen to forget anything, these people will give you the details.
One would hardly believe this statement to be true, yet it professes to state the facts. If it does-and I have no reason to doubt its veracity-I claim that the Government should see to it that this man receives compensation.
I could bring many other cases to the attention of the House such, for instance, as that of J. Alfred Mercier, who has written more than one letter to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Militia, although the then Secretary of State could obtain "no information" concerning his case. There is also the case of Edouard Tremblay, one of the saddest of all and to which I specially draw the attention of the Minister of Justice. I would say more about this young man's case were it not for the fact that my hon. friend from Charlevoix (Mr. Casgrain) will no doubt put up a strong plea in his behalf. I pass over the case of Demeule, Bergeron and Bussieres-[DOT] killed at the age of twenty.

Here we have the remarkable fact that four civilians were killed and not a single fatality happened among the forces of His Majesty. This fact would naturally lead any one to pause and reflect. There is a principle of common law laid down in the Criminal Code which declares that, if necessary, force must be met by force. It is to be found at section 53 of the Criminal Code, Cap. 146. It reads as follows:
Everyone unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked such assault, is Justified in repelling force by force, if the force he uses is not meant to cause death or grievous bodily harm, and is no more than is necessary for the purpose of self-defence.
2. Every one so assaulted is justified, though he causes death or grievous bodily harm, if he causes it under reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm from the violence with which the assault was originally made or with which the assailant pursues his purpose, and if he believes, on reasonable grounds, that he cannot otherwise preserve himself from death or grievous bodily harm.
The cases I have put before the House are the cases of men who being practically alone were shot at hy a few soldiers and killed or wounded when there was no reason whatever to think that they had had anything to do with the riots. To prove this I must refer again to the unfortunate case of Avila Blouin. I shall read a letter from him which he is willing to back up at any time that an investigation takes place, if the Government decide to grant one:
Mr. Geo. Parent, M.P.,
Quebec.
Rue Chevrifcre,
Parish of the Sacred Heart,
Quebec, P.Q.
Sir,-I wish to interest you in my case, which I am sure deserves special attention. I was unfortunate enough to be wounded on April 1, during the Quebec riots. I was hit in the right leg, and after two operations, I am obliged to walk with crutches since the leg has been amputated two inches below the knee. I declare upon my honour.that the following is the true story of the events which occurred on the above-mentioned date.
On the night of April 1, after having worked all evening at my garage at the corner of Des-glacis and D'Aguillon streets; this spot is quite remote from the scene of-the riots.
I started for home about 11.40 p.m. On arriving at the Boulevard Langlier I was ordered by two sentries to keep straight on. I had gone but a few steps when I heard a whistle, and I threw up my hands, thinking this to be the most prudent thing to do, since I understood no English. I retraced my steps, in order to make myself understood by the sentries who had just let me pass. Whilst I was in the act of turning P was fired upon and hit in the left leg. The leg was badly injured, and the soldiers wishing to prevent me from getting up, I presume, tied me to a post, in order to bandage my wound. I am under the impression that they were not quite sane, because, instead of
relieving my pain, they hit me on the head and in the face. Soon afterwards they carried me into a private house, and the military doctor gave orders for the ambulance to carry me to the Military Hospital. They amputated my leg without asking my consent or that of my parents, in spite of the fact that I had given them the telephone number of my home. T underwent treatment at the hospital for five months.
My leg was amputated twice, and I consider myself disabled to the extent of fifty per cent.
It is now impossible for me to run a garage, and I have lost all hopes of the future. My incapacity I ascribe to the fact that the operation in question was so badly performed that specialists have advised me that I will find considerable difficulty in wearing an artificial ilmb.
I wish to call your attention to the fact that it would appear from the coroner's' inquest that the officer commanding gave orders not to shoot after eleven o'clock. I was fired upon a few minutes before midnight. I was alone, and if they had any reason to suspect me they might have taken me prisoner, and there was no necessity for shooting.
Yours very sincerely,
Avila Blouin.
I have seen this unfortunate man a few times, and I must repeat, Sir, what I said last year, that his case is deserving of consideration. His daily appearance in the public streets, popular as he was and still is, bearing the evidence of the treatment he received, is no doubt a sore which cannot be cured in a day, but which will be very much alleviated if the Government comes to his rescue in the form of adequate compensation.
I will not specify any further cases. The right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) was good enough last year to say a few words concerning this matter, and from the tenor of his speech I was inclined to believe that he would find some means of indemnifying these persons. I shall quote his words because I want to have them on record. Here is what he said last year:
With regard to that proposition I can at the present moment only say-and I fancy that the strongest supporter of the motion would expect no more of me under present circumstances- that I shall certainly be glad to give consideration to it, and to approach it with a desire simply to look into the justification or lack of justification that may be found for it. Of course, even if one accepted the general proposition as being sound-that general proposition being, as I understand it, that if you assume, on the one hand that that action of the Government was not subject to criticism but was a necessary action in the general interest, and on the other hand, that the particular persons injured were perfectly innocent persons, and that under those circumstances it would be proper to assimilate the injury done to those persons to the damage suffered by individuals whose properties are taken in the general interest, and that therefore proper compensation for those injuries would be justified as being an indemnification to a party suffering by some perfectly proper action necessarily taken in the public inter-

es*-I did not, of course, come here expecting to be asked to pass a final opinion upon a question of that kind, and I can say nothing more except that I shall be glad to give consideration, and to ask my colleagues to give consideration, to the proposition that has been put forward, and to weigh carefully what has in support of that proposition been so moderately and at the same time so clearly put forward. The papers will be brought down.
I have no objection whatever to the conditions imposed by the right hon. gentleman to justify his intervention. I have not thrown any blame upon the Government, except in so far as its mind and its executive powers were permitted to be influenced by wrong advice.
A good deal of harm has been done, innocent victims have been killed and others wounded as I have stated. To point out the animus that existed at the time among the soldiers, I could have mentioned, for instance, the way Father Evain, a priest, was handled by certain soldiers at the very moment he was administering the last rites of the church to wounded civilians. I did not do so because I did not wish to appeal to racial or religious prejudices. I could have related how I myself, just as I was walking home from church on Saturday evening, was told by an officer to follow three different directions at the same time.
I could have said that the first shot fired was the act of a soldier. I could have said all this and a little more, but I do not think the purposes I have in view would be better served if I were to give more details.
One word more, Mr. Speaker, and I shall have concluded my remarks. Last year when a subject similar to the present one was discussed, the right hon. Minister of Justice expressed the view that the demands for redress appeared to come at a very late hour. The reasons for that apparent delay are obvious. When minds were inflamed, when prejudices were running high, it was not the time to present such claims as these. It was considered more advisable to wait until time had shown and proved the injustice committed. To-day Quebec is known, as it should always have been known, as a law-abiding province whose people are lovers of British institutions. Now that the province of Quebec seems to be better understood by the whole Dominion, and when she is declared to be the fairest and one of the soundest of our provinces and our compatriots are regarded as good loyal citizens -as they always have been-it is time to come back and again to claim reparation for the injustice done to them, and I believe that that injustice can only be righted by the Government of Canada as a whole.
[Hr. Parent.]
We have tried to discover who is responsible for the shooting and killing. Some lawyers advised that the city of Quebec might be responsible, and the city was sued for damages, but the court declared that the city was not liable. Other lawyers have advised that the Government of Canada is responsible. In my humble opinion it is a case for the Dominion to deal with. I think every citizen of this country should contribute towards indemnifying the innocent victims who under those sad circumstances suffered so severely.

Mr. Speaker, I second the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Quebec West (Mr. Parent), and I shall add very few words to what he has said. As to the circumstances which led up to the troubles to which he has referred and the events which occured in connection with those troubles, I do not think it is necessary to say anything. No good purpose can be served by doing so; the issue is one of the past. However, as a result of these troubles innocent victims have suffered, and my hon. friend is right in claiming that these victims are en-4 p.m. titled to compensation. The city of Quebec cannot be held responsible in any way, because they had no latitude in the matter; the military authorities had taken from them the duty of maintaining peace and order; therefore they were no longer responsible. This is the view which has been taken by the law courts, and undoubtedly it is the correct view. Men who had nothing to do either directly or indirectly with those troubles, men who were returning from their work and had to pass through certain streets of the city, were either killed or wounded, though they were connected in no way with the occurrences of that time and were not responsible in any way for them. I submit that under the circumstances the Government and the military authorities are responsible for the damage that was caused. Human life is more important than real estate or property of any kind. When in time of war a piece of property has to be taken for military purposes, compensation is always paid to the owners. I think I may fairly say that even if the military authorities were properly carrying out their functions when these lives were taken, the Government is responsible to those who suffer-even if the military authorities were right; even if what they did served the purposes of the war. I do not think any fair-minded gentleman in

this House can deny that those who suffered under such circumstances have a right to compensation. The Government ought to investigate thoroughly every case, and in all cases where lives were taken or persons wounded, when the persons in question were not responsible in any way for the troubles and had proper occasion for being where they were at the time they suffered injury, the Government owes it to the dependants of these persons, as a matter of honour, to pay to them a fair and just compensation. For these reasons I second with pleasure the motion of my hon. friend.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, allow me to say a few words on the subject of this most important resolution which is to-day before the House and was already last year submitted to its consideration. I do not desire to prolong this debate and I do not wish to repeat the arguments so ably presented last year and this year by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) and by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). Let me just call your attention to one of the cases mentioned by my hon. friend from Quebec West, the case of Edouard Tremblay, a young man who was to finish his technical school course in June, 1918. As I said,' Mr. Tremblay would have completed his course at the technical school in June, 1918. He was a son of Mrs. Mailloux, a widow, of Murray Bay, in the county of Charlevoix. At the time of the so-called Quebec riots he was spending his holidays with his family. On April 1 he returned to Quebec and, on the very same day he was shot near Bagot street. He reached Quebec by the Quebec-Saguenay railway at four o'clock in the evening, after supper, he went for a walk with one of his cousins, and it was whilst taking this walk near Bagot street, that he was shot through the leg and elbow and died shortly after. The inquest showed positively that neither of the wounds could have caused death; according to Dr. Marois' own words, at the coroner's inquest: "The wounds were not sufficient, to cause death." In fact, if in this circumstance, there had been available an ambulance, or some one to give first aid, his case would not have proved so serious; this boy would still be living, and helping his mother to earn a living, as it is done in the province of Quebec, and in the county which I have the honour to represent in this House. He was shot about ten o'clock, and it was not until one o'clock in the morning that he was attended to by Dr. Marois himself. Unfortunately, he was
already in a very weak condition, and it was too late. He died the next morning, at eight o'clock, without having recovered consciousness.
Mr. Speaker, I am well acquainted with young Tremblay's family; his uncle, Mr. Arthur Blackburn, is a well-known citizen of Murray Bay, and I have every reason to believe that this young man, who was quietly on his way to see some of his relatives, had in no way whatever transgressed the law or endeavoured to participate in the riots in question. Besides, at the coroner's inquest, where all the facts were proven, no evidence of this kind was given.
I believe that this case, as well as the others which have been submitted to the House by the hon. member for Quebec West, prove clearly that on this occasion there were innocent victims who were either wounded or killed, or who sustained losses. We have but to look back to our history to find that there have been other such disturbances. In 1837, for instance, after many appeals and great difficulties of all kinds, the government had to acknowledge the claims put forward by the respresenta-tives of the people, and if I remember well, an Act was passed by Parliament by which a compassionate allowance was granted to all those who had sustained losses during the rebellion of 1837. What is happening in the different countries of the world? Take those countries, for instance, which are not as civilized as our beautiful Dominion of Canada, countries where disturbances and riots recur from year to year; such, for example, is the case in Mexico. A press despatch from that country, which I read in an English paper, the other day, says that General Obregon, who has just assumed the direction of public affairs, is endeavouring to re-establish order and peace, and one of his first measures will have for its object to compensate the rebels who have suffered from any loss whatever, those who have been wounded or whose relatives have been killed. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if a country like Mexico takes into consideration the fact that there may have been losses of life or of money, and if such a country is ready to compensate even those who have caused the rebellion and have taken part in it, there is all the more reason, in a case where quiet and peaceful citizens like the victims of the Quebec riots-case which has been submitted to Parliament by the hon. members for Quebec West and Quebec East-as well as in the case which I have just mentioned myself. I think that the Government should accede to the re-

quest of the hon. member for Quebec West and adopt this resolution. This would only be a fair measure, a measure of equity, and at the present moment, it would be a good policy on the part of the Government. I therefore appeal to all members of the Government, and to those who support them, to vote in favour of this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent), upon the persistence with which he has brought forward this question during the course of this Parliament. It was my pleasure last year to follow the hon. gentleman when he explained in such a clear manner the claim of the wounded and of the dependents of the killed in the famous Quebec riots. Having listened, last year, after his clear exposition, to the answer given to him by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), I came to the conclusion that the Government, immediately after the session came to an end, would investigate the whole matter. I find, however, this session that nothing whatever has been done. The question, apparently, has been treated in a light manner; it seems to me, at all events, that the subject has been discarded, as it were, by the Minister of Justice as being of insufficient importance to engage the close attention of the Government. These riots are more or less a family affair, I mean a Canadian affair; they are one of the regrettable legacies of the war. The war, indeed, in Europe, has amassed any amount of miseries, and it would be expected that that should be the case, because the continent of Europe was the actual theatre of the operations of the war. The miseries that have been accumulated in Europe, it will take, probably, centuries to repair. The Treaty of Peace has endeavoured to repair the damages and losses suffered during the war as between the allied nations and the enemy countries; but as my right hon. friend is well aware, the Treaty of Peace has not, in any instance, attempted to repair any damage or inconvenience that might have been caused by one country to its own resortissants, as my right hon. friend would say. It remains the duty of the government concerned in each country to see that, if any damages or losses have been suffered by some of their Nationals, they should take the proper step to right the wrongs that have been caused.
IMr. Casgrain.]
It is not my intention to rehearse the different cases which have been cited by the hon. member for Quebec West, but I think the House will be unanimous in coming to the conclusion that the relation of facts as presented by that hon. member is impressive; in a word, the situation is like this: You are a peaceable citizen; you are going from the place of your occupation to the place of your residence or domicile; on your way home, you meet an attack on the part of His Majesty's soldiers, although you are in no degree guilty of any offence; as a result of this attack, which may not have been absolutely voluntary on the part of the soldiers, but which may have been a result of their orders, you suffer a disability, or you incur death. This, in short, is what happened. If it is not so, let the Government find out. Can the statements made by the hon. member for Quebec West be sustained by evidence? This is the whole question. If those statements can be sustained, who amongst the hon. members who sit in this House would deny the right of those who suffered to be indemnified in some degree? This argument appears absolutely clear to me. This is not a provincial question; I am not drawn into this debate by the fact that the riots have taken place in the city of Quebec, with which I am, perhaps, better acquainted than any other city in Canada. That the same things occurred in the sad situation that developed some two years ago in the city of Winnipeg, had any of the Winnipeg citizens suffered injury or death from the action of the soldiers of His Majesty in their efforts to re-establish order, my position and my contention would be absolutely the same. This is not a question of provincialism, nor of race, nor of politics; those conditions must be put absolutely out of the mind of every hon. member. The principle appears to me to be right, that, if the soldiers of His Majesty have committed a wrong, the Government, the Parliament, the country as a whole, must right the wrong.
There is more than the question of principle involved. What about the question of national interest? Is it not of paramount importance in Canada that the most modest citizen be firmly convinced that, if he or she, suffers an injury from the constituted authorities, reparation will be made? It is, I think, of much concern to us also that this sentiment should prevail in Canada

amongst all citizens, regardless of their situation. I will not press the point any further; but I would urge the right hon. gentleman who presides over the Department of Justice to institute an investigation into this case in order to find out whether the statements of the hon. member for Quebec West are well founded, and if they are well founded, the question is then one of honour, one of equity, and more than that, one of national interest, as I tried to demonstrate a minute ago. I shall say no more on this subject except to congratulate again my hon. friend from Quebec West (Mr. Parent), and to commend to the House his persistence and tenacity of purpose in bringing this case before Parliament. In doing so, he is serving not only his electors, but Canada as a whole.

I am sorry that I was not present at the opening of this debate and so missed hearing my hon. friend from Quebec West (Mr. Parent). I was otherwise engaged in attempting to convince the Government that in order to avoid further claims for compensation something should be done to prevent the rocks from falling on the inhabitants of another portion of our city. However, I listened with considerable attention to the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and to the other members who have taken part in this debate, and I heartily concur in what they have said.
Without entering into a discussion of the causes, either proximate or otherwise, of the famous Quebec riots, I think we all agree after hearing the evidence so ably presented by the hon. member for Quebec West that there were undoubtedly a large number of innocent victims of these riots. So far as a case of which I have personal knowledge is concerned, a gentlman who lives in my constituency was, at the time he was wounded, walking along the street at some distance from the scene of any riot or trouble. He was a member of a family which had given several sons to the war, one of whom had been killed at the front, so his sympathies, if any, would most assuredly not have been with people of a riotous or rebellious disposition.
We have, on the other hand, this point of view to take into consideration. Hon. gentlemen will remember that at the time of the riots the whole country was very much stirred up. We had flaming head lines in the newspapers from coast to coast,
which seemed to indicate that in the city of Quebec an actual state of warfare existed. Naurally, the soldiers sent from outside points-and a large number of them came from other provinces-were somewhat influenced by these inflammatory reports. I am in a position to state that a large number of these soldiers were raw rcruits, that some of them had never had Ross rifles in their hands before the evening on which they arrived at Quebec. Some of them even-and I can give authority for this statement-had received Ross rifles and had been issued with ball ammunition for the first time in their lives only ten minutes before they marched to Jacques Cartier Square in the city of Quebec. A large number of them, in shooting, I have no doubt, acted contrary to the orders which they had received. Taking these things into consideration, the state of mind in which these raw recruits must have found themselves, the reports which they must have heard, their obvious inexperience in the handling of dangerous weapons and placed in such a situation as they were, I think, without in any way imputing any blame to the soldiers themselves, that some blame must attach to those that sent them there. If, as will no doubt be urged by hon. gentlemen opposite, there were no other troops available, that does not in any way help the case of those who are of the opinion that no compensation should be paid. We have here, at any rate, on the facts of the case, shown that there was some negligence on the part of some one in authority, that certain well behaved citizens were injured, and some unfortunately killed. We have it that all precautions in the way of sending experienced men were not taken, and we have the inflamed state of public opinion at that time. So it seems to me that a case for compensation for the victims has been made by the hon. member for Quebec West, and I think the Minister of Justice would only be doing simple justice to the victims and their families if he would give this matter more serious consideration than he has hitherto given to it. He would at the same time, as my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) has said, be confirming in the minds of the citizens of Canada that opinion which they have always had, and which they should have, that for any damage to which they have been subjected on the part of any one in authority they should be fully and amply compensated.

Mr. HORATIO C. HOCKEN (West Toronto) : My hon. friends opposite have spread a good deal of salve over this incident in respect of which they are asking compensation for men who were injured. What they are asking is practically a pension for rioters, for men who were on the streets, in the midst of a riot, after they had been warned by General Lessard that they should not be there. Nobody can claim, by any stretch of the imagination, that men injured under such circumstances have any legal right to compensation. If I understand the arguments put forth, one of the men lost half his earning power, and therefore his demand will be for a fifty per-cent pension. This man, who was injured in a riot at home when this country was being urged to raise a sufficient number of men to support our troops at the front, was with his friends rioting on the streets of a Canadian city. My hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) says that this is a family question, a Canadian question. No, Sir, it is a French Canadian question, for in no other part of this country was there anything of the kind. There was unanimity everywhere else in support of our men at the front. The men who refused to be warned and went out and joined in a riot of this kind at the most critical time in the history of our country and empire have no right to come to this Parliament and ask for an indemnity for wounds or any thing else that they suffered. They went there deliberately; with their eyes open, they engaged in an unlawful assembly and if they have suffered any loss it should be made up to them, if by anybody, by either the province of Quebec or the city of Quebec. The people of the other ' provinces of Canada, who contributed so enormously in men and in money, and made such tremendous sacrifices to save this country from the Hun, should not be called upon to contribute in the slightest degree to indemnify men who played the part of rebels at that critical period in our history. There is no moral right, there is no legal right. I cannot imagine how any man can bring a question of this kind before Parliament. It is probable that it will be brought up in the House year in and year out until we have a Government supine enough to heed the plea; but I cannot conceive of a Parliament composed of men such as are here to-day passing this motion. To my mind it would be a disgrace if this motion were carried. It would arouse among the Great War Veterans throughout

the country, as well as among people who have suffered so seriously through the war, a sense of resentment that would be expressed in no uncertain manner against any Government or any party that would be gulity of an act so entirely without justification.

May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question?
Yes, sir.

Did you say that the
hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent), was asking the Government for compensation for rioters?
I say that.
Well, I deny that entirely.
You are wrong.

I say that these men
had been warned, just as though the mayor of the city had read the Riot Act. They were warned by proclamation to keep off the streets. They refused to obey the proclamation, they went into the crowd, and if they suffered under those circumstances it was entirely their own fault.
Do you still claim that they were rioters?
I claim that they were among the rioters.
Oh, "among".
They had no right to be among the rioters, because they were warned by public proclamation not to go out.

It was not my intention to intervene in this debate, nor do I purpose taking up more than a minute or two. I merely wish to draw attention to the free and easy way in which the hon. gentleman who has just concluded (Mr. Hocken), ignores the crux of the matter brought before the House. In characteristic Toronto fashion he misrepresented the statements made by my hon. friend from Quebec West regarding the merits of this case. My hon. friend from Quebec West read a number of statements from the survivors in whose behalf compensation was claimed. As I recall the cases that were cited, they were either those of men peaceably engaged in their places of business, or going peaceably through the streets on their way home after business. One man in particular-I think, the man whose case was first mentioned by the hon.

member for Quebec West,-told about his premises having been entered by men wearing the uniform of soldiers, and of the attacks made upon him in his store. Yet, in the face of the evidence submitted through my hon. friend in connection with that case, the hon. gentleman from Toronto (Mr. Hocken), bulks all these people together and refers to them as rioters who were on the streets when they had no business to be there. How does he make a man a rioter who is attacked in his place of business? But that is the characteristic Toronto style of dealing with facts.
Hear, hear, but they are not all like that; I know.

Then he went on to
allege that these people went out in the streets and joined in a riot. Now, listening attentively to the evidence submitted by my hon. friend from Quebec West, I did not hear the name of one man mentioned who had joined in a riot. Each of the men injured was wounded while engaged in some peaceful occupation, or while proceeding quietly along the street. My hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), mentioned a matter which I do not recall having heard in any of the preceding discussions of this unfortunate incident. He mentioned that the military authorities had superseded the civil authorities on the occasion in question and had taken the administration of law and order into their own hands. If that be the case, then I submit that that fact alone would afford my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), and the Government of which he is a member, a ground for action, if nothing else did. In any event, in view of the interpretation sought to be placed upon the incident by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken),-an interpretation which, during this week or the following week, will be blazoned forth in large print on the front page of the newspaper with which the hon. gentleman is inseparably associated-I submit that it is a duty which the Government owes it to the people to perform,-I say this with all due respect, and without any desire to dictate to my right hon. friend at all-to see that the evidence bearing on this incident shall be fully elicited in some formal way. When that has been done, I am sure Parliament and the country will be satisfied with whatever action may follow afterwards.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) :
speechtext:
If ever there was a
question before Parliament which should be approached calmly and dispassionately, and without any party feeling, it is a question of this character. We as British subjects pride ourselves on the fact that every man who casts his lot and his allegiance under the British flag shall always have a square deal, a fair show, and an impartial trial, if there is anything to be tried. I think, therefore, that this high court of Parliament would make a mistake if it approached any case before the full facts were available in a proper and conclusive form, so far as they can be made conclusive in a matter of this kind. The facts set forth by the hon. member for Quebec West impressed me very much, and I was shocked to find that such a thing as described, could take place in this Canada of ours. We all have a high sense of the liberties of the subject, and we should be able with good reason to declare that every man, woman and child can at all times, at any hour in the day or in the night, move about in any part of this country, and particularly on the streets of a city of the size of Quebec, without the slightest fear of molestation in any way. That is a fact which we are apt to take for granted. Now, if it is true that in the city of Quebec some time during the war assaults were made on peaceful citizens, that men's shops were broken into, business interfered with, goods practically stolen, and those in charge of business places assaulted, then that is a matter for investigation; and if, as a result of inquiry, it were found that these things did- actually take place, there are only two courses of action:	Somebody should pay
those who lost their goods, and the criminal responsible should be brought to justice and treated in accordance with the nature of the crime of which he might be found guilty. The fact that a man is wearing a uniform, and is permitted to carry a gun, does not relieve him of criminality in this country if he does anything wrong which he is not ordered to do. As I understand the law, the military power of this country can only be called to the aid of the civil authorities in a certain way, and when conditions are such that the civil authorities are no longer able to mantain order. If conditions of that kind arise in Canada proper orders are given, and the Minister of Militia orders out a certain number of troops to the aid of the civil authorities. If that happened in this instance then, as I understand it, that military force was subject to the orders, discipline and direction of the civil

authority in the city of Quebec, and that authority is responsible for anything that may have ensued from the issuance of those orders. But if a body of men, sent into the city of Quebec by the Dominion, had broken away from authority, I would be disposed to think that the Government and Parliament, as the central authority to which those men are subject, would be liable, I would say in a general way, for anything done by those men contrary to law. The matter is one that should be fully inquired into and the facts properly placed before Parliament. I would regret indeed if any province or an individual from one province or another, should, for one moment, try to stir up trouble over this matter. The facts should be investigated by some properly constituted court whose findings, when presented to Parliament, would not be questioned. I would submit to the Government that if any inquiry is to be made it should be conducted by parties regarded as highly competent, and absolutely removed from any partisan or other influence that would cause them to make any report but such as would be in absolute conformity with the facts. That having been done, I trust this Parliament would rise to the occasion and treat the case on its merits. The impression should never be allowed to go forth, whatever the reason might be which created the situation, that our citizens might be assaulted with impunity, and some of them killed, without the proper authorities taking cognizance of the matter and doing something to compensate the sufferers for the depredations that were committed. Such, I am sure, will not be permitted here. No person, I am certain, will ever be allowed to say, with any degree of truth, that he was not treated fairly and in an absolutely just manner by the authorities of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a matter of some regret to me that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), followed in like manner by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent), should have assumed that this matter was treated lightly by the Minister of Justice, and that it had not received the attention, and had not been looked into. I only have to say in that regard that both gentlemen are entirely mistaken.
We are glad to hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
After the discussion of last year when I intimated that I would look into the matter, I received some three

claims. These did not include a claim for the breaking into of anybody's shop, nor if my memory serves me, a claim on behalf of a man named Mercier, who was mentioned. In regard to those cases I understand there was an inquiry made by the Militia Department, at least I am so informed. Touching the three cases that came before me I was at pains, so far as my time and capacity enabled me to do so, to look into the law on the question, and I also had the law officers of the department do the same, and I reached the conclusion-the conclusion is one, I am satisfied, that hon. gentlemen opposite who are lawyers, if they also will look into the matter, will inevitably come to-that there can be no question of legal responsibility in the matter. We may as well lay that feature aside at once, and put it out of the question. I venture to say it is perfectly clear. Where the military authority intervenes, the soldier, because he is a soldier has not any more right than any person else to use unnecessary force for the maintenance of peace. If he does more, and it is a wrongful act, he has his responsibility for it; but there is, as a matter of law, I do not hesitate to say, no legal responsibility upon the Crown. I said last year I was impressed with the argument made by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), and which I think was supported by other hon. gentlemen, in which it was sought to establish an analogy between the case of the expropriation, for public purposes, of a man's property, where the principle is recognized that it implies an obligation of compensation, and the case where-without imputing blame to anybody-a man's life is taken by an operation necessary for the public good. I must confess that I have not been able to find anything to support that proposition; so I think we have to approach this question-I at all events am forced to do so-accepting of the position that I am not face to face with a legal claim, with a claim susceptible of being legally established or maintained by a court. Hon. gentlemen are exceedingly sympathetic with the persons whom they represent as affected, and who they represent to be absolutely innocent people. Of course, I do not suppose it would be suggested that if that assumption were not sound there could be any question of discussing from any point of view a claim advanced by people who themselves were guilty of taking part in the riots that required to be suppressed or of unduly exposing themselves with knowledge; but the

case, I take it, is put forward upon the assumption that the people concerned were absolutely innocent victims. Even assuming that to be so, we are not face to face with a claim enforceable in law, at all events I can find anything nothing to justify that view.
As I have said, hon. gentlemen opposite are exceedingly sympathetic with the sufferings of these people and, if the facts are as they have been representing them to be, I can quite understand the existence of that sympathy. But my hon. friends are in position to indulge their sympathy to the full; I am not. Whatever might be my sympathy-and assuming perfect innocence on his part surely I would sympathize with a person, who, without fault of any kind, unfortunately lost his life, or was subjected to grievous injury; under the circumstances I think I would sympathize as fully as hon. gentlemen do-I have a duty to perform-and my function is to advise as to the legal responsibilities of this Government. Now I did, as I have said, go into this matter and I had my law officers go into it, and I have before me their report which confirms the only conclusion I was able to arrive at myself. So, clearly, I at all events have to take that position, and I do it with a very considerable degree of confidence that I am not mistaken.
We are not face to face with a question of legal responsibility. Then the question arises, how far are we to go? I have to remember when I am listening to this very impressive appeal to sympathy from hon. gentlemen, that it is not an appeal to me for payment of my own money; it is an appeal for payment of the money of this country. Now, am I or are hon. gentlemen themselves entitled to ask, because of their sympathy with people who have no legal claim against the Government, that the moneys of this country should be paid to those people in compensation of injuries sustained? It is not the only case where in law and in justice damage may be suffered and nobody be responsible for it; hon gentlemen, I suppose, are all perfectly familiar with what is often described in very barbarous Latin as damnum absque injuria. So far as this Government is concerned while these people may have suffered damage, and may be quite innocent sufferers, there is no wrongdoing established on the part of the Government, and that is absolutely essential as a basis of legal responsibility.
That is the doctrine that the Crown can do wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Crown has no responsibility for the wrong-doing of its individual employees. If you acknowledged any other principle there would be practically no limit to the possible liability of the Crown. Assuming it could be established that the soldiers were in some respects at fault, those particular soldiers, of course, have their responsibility. If the officer commanding unlawfully ordered certain things to be done, he has his responsibility. But you cannot pass that off onto the Crown. There are cases, of course, where a Government, acknowledging no responsibility, does feel justified in granting what are called compassionate allowances. But let me point out in that connection that the city of Quebec is not the only city where difficulties arose which gave rise to complaints by reason of the action of soldiers. We had such claims emanating from people in the city of Calgary amounting to very considerable sums.
Was that during the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
My hon. friend from Toronto does not appear to know about that.
They were not rebelling against the authority of the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Those complaints referred to soldiers breaking into some man's shop. I do not know that there had been any previous rioting on the part of the citizens concerned. We had to take the same position in regard to all these claims, that they were all governed by the same general principle. Perhaps it is not necessary for an hon. member to say it, but of course a question of this kind cannot be made a question as between provinces or races or classes; there has to be one law and one rule for everybody.
Now, under that law, unfortunately there are cases of suffering and damage in different parts of the country. In regard to all such cases I and the officers of the department who are advising this Government as to its liability have to advise in accordance with the law as we find it, and I think it will be readily understood how dangerous it would be for us to undertake to view cases from the compassionate standpoint. It is not the function of a lawyer at all events to be compassionate-indeed, some wicked people say that in order to be a good lawyer one should have a bad heart and a good stomach. I do not know whether I meet those two requirements or not and whether the badness of my heart is as



great as it ought to be to make me a good lawyer, but it is undoubtedly true that, acting as the adviser of this Government, it is not possible for me to allow any sympathetic feeling to influence my advice. As I said when this matter was brought up last year, I was very much struck by the suggestion of the possible analogy between the case of the expropriation of a man's property and the case where a Government doing something for the public good does incidentally, through its employees or officers, deprive some one of his life- an analogy which would justify from the legal standpoint the granting of compensation. The best examination that I have been able to make has led me to the conclusion that that analogy cannot be sustained.
Eliminating absolutely the question of legal responsibility, and treating the appeal as based upon considerations of commiseration, I have to remember that all my colleagues have not had the advantage of hearing that appeal, and while I cannot, in view of what I have said, do otherwise than oppose this particular motion, I shall be glad to bring to their attention what has been said this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed this debate with some interest. If from the purely legal point of view there is not in the judgment of my right hon. friend a case for compensation of the victims of the Quebec riots, I believe that when we consider what is called in law the res gestae, there is good ground for at least a compassionate allowance to those victims. I have not the cases at hand, but I believe if my right hon. friend will delve into the precedents of the Department of Justice under the Union of the two Canadas he will find that at the time of the Gavazzi riots in Montreal, compensation was given by the Government to the victims of the military on that occasion. If my memory serves me well, my right hon. friend will also take up Justin McCarthy's "History of Our Own Times" and peruse the chapter dealing with the Gordon riots in England, there he will find that the Home Government compensated some of the victims.
Let us take a case which is probably more familiar to my right hon. friend, a case in which the Crown came
5 p.m. to the rescue of men who had no legal claim for compensation. I refer to the case of the squatters at Fox Bay, on Anticosti Island. These squatters

had been on that island, and that particular part of the island, for many years, but Anally the owner' of the island demanded that they be deported; that the squatters leave the particular place where they had located. There was not one tittle of evidence that the squatters were entitled to any compensation. Yet the Dominion Government-and I believe the law officers of the Crown advised accordingly-decided that the squaters should be compensated in some way. As a matter of fact, the squatters did leave the island of Anticosti and were given by the Department of the Interior letters patent in respect of lands in the West in order to compensate them for the semblance of title which they imagined they had by virtue of their having for many years lived at Fox Bay on the Island of Anticosti. My right hon. friend was impressed last year by the appeal which was made by my hon. friend from Quebec, on the ground that there was some similarity between the cases brought forward by my hon. friend and cases of expropriation. I believe that the case of the squatters of Fox Bay should have some influence on the final decision arrived at by the Government in this matter. It was not a question of law; it was a question of equity, of fair play-of British fair play, I might say to my hon. friend from Toronto West (Mr. Hocken). It was a question of compassionate allowance. I find that on several occasions this Parliament has ignored the strict letter of the law and voted sums of money on the ground that there was occasion for granting compassionate allowance. Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to come back to the particular events which took place in 1917, and in reverting to that phase of the discussion I wish to be as moderate as I can. It is not necessary to rekindle old fires; I believe we are all anxious to have peace not only in this wide world, but more so in our own country, Canada. My right hon. friend will remember that the cause of this whole trouble was the announcement suddenly made that we were to have compulsory military service. Are you going to blame very seriously the young men of this country because they at first resented the application of that law? Of course, every man must obey the law of the land. But, Mr. Speaker, it is the privilege of the young men of my race to be very logical. My right hon. friend will admit that the French mind is generally logical. The young men had been told-indeed, a solemn pledge had been taken before Parliament

and before the country-that there would be no compulsory service in Canada; that enlistments would be under the voluntary system. But suddenly this was changed. We live in a free country, Mr. Speaker. We rejoice in the fact that we have free political institutions, and naturally it was the privilege of the yeomanry to criticize and to protest. The young men of Quebec criticized and protested, and they were not alone in doing so; other men in other parts of the country criticized and protested. And if finally that feature of the political situation in 1917 was accepted in other parts of Canada, you well know, Mr Speaker, and every conscientious member of this House well knows, that it was because the promise was made to these young men of Ontario and the West that they would not be conscripted; that the law would apply only to the young men of the province of Quebec. Sir, it is too soon yet to begin writing the history of the war, but When that history comes to be written, I make bold to say that the historian will give justice to whom justice is due. I was telling my right hon. friend a moment ago that, one must remember the peculiar circumstances of the application of the Military Service Act; one must take into consideration what the criminalists call res gestae. Let us remember the inflammatory speeches delivered throughout the whole country, the incendiary writings published broadcast, the appeals made on all sides, for and against. Let us bear in mind-and this has been admitted since-that the people of the old city of Quebec are a law-abiding and liberty-loving people. All of a sudden, on the very day when the churches of that city were packed full of pious people, the Ontario soldiers appeared and began tramping in the streets. Remember that it was on Holy Friday in the city of Quebec, a God-fearing city, if there is one on this continent, that regiments sent from Ontario started marching. Poor soldiers! They were doing their duty as they knew it; they were obeying the orders as they were given to them. Who will ever believe that the soldiers, who came from Ontario to restore order on Holy Friday in the city of Quebec, did believe in their heart and soul that there was any order to be restored in that city on that particular day? But, elsewhere, there were men anxious, indeed, to send soldiers into Quebec during that period of inflammatory speeches throughout Canada, in 96J
order to serve the political ends, we know. The situation in Quebec, I say to my right hon. friend, on the morning of Holy Friday in 1918, is on a par with the situation prepared, abetted, concocted by other agitators, at the time of the raid on the Guelph Novitiate. We all know for what purpose that raid was organized, and all liberty-loving Canadians were humiliated by what happened on that occasion.
My right hon. friend says that no compensation can be given under such circumstances. It has been stated that law-abiding citizens, who were not rioters, lost their lives, that others lost property. I have in mind a case which came up before the criminal courts of Montreal, where young men were brought under the criminal law before their peers because they had threatened to destroy by dynamite the residence of Lord Atholstan at Cartierville, near Montreal. The Department of Justice must have been represented when that trial took place. At all events, my right hon. friend will remember that it was established before Mr. Justice Pelletier, a4nd the twelve jurors, that the chief, the star witness of the Crown was a man by the name of Desjardins and that that man had received money from the Department of Justice. It was also proven that Desjardins received $25 and acted as "agent provocateur."

He was bonded by
them and defended by their attorney.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The man was employed. That he was employed as an "agent provocateur," is another statement, and that certainly is not true.

I will ask my right hon. friend-I am sure he is speaking in good faith-to read over the evidence in that case. He will find that Mr. Justice Pelletier, one of his former colleagues, who presided over the assizes, was so dumbfounded that he at once adjourned the court. Read his address to the jury. Later on, this man Desjardins was arrested, and he was bonded by the Crown. Later on again he was found guilty of highway robbery, or I do not know what other crime, in the district of Hull.
Defended again by the Government.
He was defended by one of the Crown's attorneys, I am informed.
It is true.

He was sentenced to jail or penitentiary, and he is now out under ticket-of-leave. Is that a fact or not a fact? If it be true that jailbirds of that ilk were employed and paid by the Department of Justice as "agents provocateurs" for political reasons of the lowest and meanest order, is there not ground at least for the innocent victims of the Quebec riots to claim a compassionate allowance from the Government? "Oh," the hon. member for Toronto West says, "the whole country would revolt against such an idea." I do not expect that this year or next year or the year after, the victims of the Quebec riots will be indemnified. It takes some time, even in British countries, for justice to be achieved; in some countries there is no hope for justice, but under the British flag, as I read history, justice is sure to triumph. Some day, Sir, when there is a better feeling between the various races and provinces in Canada, the victims of those riots and their families will be indemnified.
Canada has passed through other crucial tests in the past. Our forefathers passed through the rebellion in Upper Canada, in Lower Canada. The forebears of the hon. member for Toronto West were not slow in exacting from the Crown, after 1837 and 1838, an indemnity for the Loyalists, and the indemnity was granted by a majority in Parliament. Years went on, and went on, and finally a patriot from Upper Canada, by the name of Robert Baldwin, took office. He allied himself with Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine. They brought peace, harmony, order, into the country, and in 1849, under the Baldwin-Lafontaine government, the families of the rebels and some of the rebels themselves were indemnified for losses incurred during the rebellion. There were some protests at the time. The Hockens of the day bet fire to the Parliament Buildings in Montreal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member must realize that his remark is hardly Parliamentary.

Let us say, the Orange Sentinels of the day set fire to the parliament buildings in Montreal. They even treated with very scant respect the person of the Governor General of the day, Lord Elgin. I have myself seen in England, in the family of Lord Elgin, a big stone which was found in the carriage of His Excellency after he left the Parliament buildings in Montreal. It was exhibited somewhere in London-a souvenir of the

loyal Sentinels of 1849. Some day too there will be a bill of indemnity to cover the damages inflicted on innocent victims of the Quebec riots, and people will then realize that the so-called riots were caused first by agents provocateurs in the pay of political agitators and secondly by the swaggering and bullying attempts of some very superior people to dominate a minority; The young men were only exercising a right by protesting against a law which they had been promised by the Prime Minister would never be enacted by this Parliament, Sir, we owe it to our dead in Flander's fields to put an end to all these causes of friction. They did not fight, they did not die, to let people like my hon. friend from West Toronto fill the air with their song of hate in Canada. They fought and they died so that their fellow-countrymen, of both races, might hereafter replace the song of hate by a song of love.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice, when he has time, and is far from the sinister influence now around him, will again scrutinize closely the cases which have been so ably brought before the House by my hon. friend from Quebec West, and I have no hesitation in saying that I believe his better judgment will be in favour of a compassionate allowance for these unhappy victims of the so-called Quebec riots.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough) :

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE

speechtext:
Hon. RODOLPHE _LEMIEUX (Maison-neuve and Gaspe) moved:
For a copy of all papers and correspondence concerning the application to the Board of Pension Commissioners of Mrs. Brunelle, widowed mother of the late Sergeant Major N. Brunelle, No. 62068, for a pension.
He said: I shall be very brief in presenting the case of the widow Brunelle. She is the mother of Sergeant-Major N. Brunelle, who enlisted in the 22nd Battalion, on December 4, 1914, and was discharged on May 21, 1919, being medically unfit owing to chronic bronchitis. He was examined at the North Bay district office of the Pension Commissioners and was awarded a pension of 25 per cent. I may say, en passant, that this young man, who enlisted at the beginning of the war and served until 1919, was awarded a decoration on the battlefield. He was 26 years of age at his death. After his return to Canada, he died on July 3, 1919, at Swastika, in northern Ontario, by accidental drowning.

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext: How long was that after he had been discharged from the army?

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext: He was discharged on May 21, 1919, when he was given a pension of 25 per cent.

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext: Disability?

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext:
Yes, and he was drowned on July 3, 1919. It will be seen that he did not long enjoy the pension granted him. When he was found after the accident a coroner living at a great distance from Swastika was summoned and held an inquest which, I may say, was all on hearsay evidence, for no one could say how the accident had occurred, except that it was during a very hot spell of weather when this young man and some companions took a bath in the river. In some way Brunelle got beyond his depth and was drowned. His mother is a widow. She is in poor in health; in fact she is absolutely helpless, being obliged to go from house to house, looking for work. She has two young daughters to take care of, and within the past few weeks, one of them, unfortunately, was nearly killed by a street car in Ottawa. So that this woman is altogether helpless. I appeared on her behalf before the Pension Commissioners and stated that in view of this man's disability and the fact that he had been incapacitated on the battlefield, the presumption was that he came to his death because he was not strong enough to cope with a situation in which a man in ordinary health would have been safe. He was sub-normal. I was referred, of course, to subsection 1 of section 11 of the Act which reads as follows:
The Commission shall award pensions to, or in respect of members of the Forces who have suffered disability in accordance with the rates set out in Schedule "A" of this Act, and, in respect of the members of the Forces who have died in accordance with the rates set out in Schedule "B" of this Act, when the disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made, is attributable to military service.
My contention is that this death, caused by an accident, is above all chiefly attributable to the military service of the unfortunate Brunelle. He came back from the battlefield with twenty-five per cent less of his fighting power, and therefore I contend that his mother should receive the pension with which, if he had been alive, he would have helped her. It is a very sad case, and I hope the Government will instruct the Committee on Pensions to report in favour of so amending the Act as to enable a case of this nature to be dealt with by the Pension Commissioners. I wish to inform the House that the coroner's inquest has revealed nothing which should prevent the mother of this young Brunelle from receiv-

ing a pension. His death resulted from an accident in the river, and the presumption in law is, that if he had been in the physical condition in which he was before he became incapacitated on the battlefield he would certainly have been able to escape that fatal accident.

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext:
The minister
under whom the Pension Commissioners act, in liason with the Government, is not at present in his place. The case as stated by my hon. friend is largely one that appeals to the sympathy, but he has also stated that the Pension Commissioners do not find that it comes within the law and they, of course, have to strictly administer the regulations according to the law. The pensions that have been arranged, even with their conditions and limitations are, I think, on a very generous scale-

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext: No doubt about it.

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext: ^but there will always be cases, even outside of that generous provision, which seem to involve very great hardship and appeal to the sympathy of individuals who become acquainted with them. It is, I suppose, absolutely impossible to frame a law which will cover all cases. I do not understand that my hon. friend finds any fault with the Board of Pension Commissioners, who have acted according to their rendering of the law and the regulations made thereunder. My hon. friend, however, as I understand, asks that they may be instructed to apply for amendments to the law, which would cover a case like this. I am not quite sure that that would be a wise procedure; but it might be possible that cases of this kind should be taken into account by the committee of the House which at present is sitting. I do not understand that my hon friend has presented this case to that Committee, but it would seem to me to be a fair method of procedure to bring it to the attention of the chairman. However, my hon. friend has placed his case on Hansard and I will call the attention of the proper minister to it.

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext:
I may add just a word to what the minister has said. I am only sorry that the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), who is the chairman of the Pensions Committee, is not at present in the House, because, he perhaps, more ably than myself, could have explained the better course for my hon. friend to
have followed. The case that the hon. friend has cited is a pathetic one, and there are a number of others that are similar. The Board of Pension Commissioners are confronted with almost innumerable cases of that kind; but that Board is a tribunal unlike any other in Canada-there is no appeal from it, it is a sovereign Board. It is only fair to add that the Pension Commissioners, so far as I have been able to judge, always give the benefit of the doubt in exercising their discretion, and it is, I think, a fair Board. It is customary, however, in cases such as my hon. friend has outlined, to refer them to the Pensions Committee. That committee have appointed a sub-committee-called the "special cases sub-committee"-which deals with all these peculiar and pathetic cases which may be brought before them. I need not mention the names of the hon. members who compose this sub-committee-they are eminently qualified for the position-and I understand that the Board of Pension Commissioners in a case like this would abide by the recommendation of the sub-committee supported by the committee as a whole. I would therefore advise my hon. friend to report the case to the committee, and it will be dealt with in due course.

subtopic: THE CASE OF SERGEANT-MAJOR N. BRUNELLE
speechtext:
I certainly will accept the advice given by my right hon. friend the acting leader of the House, and my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland). I think indeed, that as the special committee are sitting during the session they would have no objection to hearing whatever complaints are made by the families of the soldiers. In the present instance, I wish to emphasize, that I do not find fault with the commission; far from it; they have treated me with the utmost courtesy and have taken a good deal of their time in going over the whole record. I spent a morning with them, and they were absolutely fair in their dealings with me. But, as the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) has stated, here is a case which just touches the edge of the law and yet cannot come within the law, because the law itself is not elactic enough to cover it. However, every one will admit the hardship. Here is a man who was disabled, receiving a pension of twenty-five per cent; he is drowned in the river; there is no coroner's inquest to speak of except to view the body and say that it was found in the water. Is there not a legal presumption, Mr. Speaker, that this man was drowned because he was not able

to look after himself as presumably he would have done had he been fully normal? [DOT]He received his pension in the month of May, the drowning accident took place in the month of July. He was the only support of his widowed mother. Now she is penniless and left with two young girls, one of whom is crippled as a result of an accident on the street railway in Ottawa. And yet the Pension Commissioners tell me that the law cannot provide for such a case. I accept the advice of my hon. friend from Beauce-I will appear before the committee with widow Brunelle.

Motion agreed to.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

subtopic: COMPLAINT OF DR. BURNHAM AGAINST SIBERIAN GOVERNMENT
COMPLAINT OF DR. BURNHAM AGAINST SIBERIAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
For a copy of all Correspondence exchanged between the Canadian Government and the Serbian Government concerning the expulsion of Dr. Burnham[DOT] and his Hospital Mission from Montenegro.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the old parliamentary struggles between the King and the Commons the Speaker could not leave the Chair before the grievances of the people were ventilated. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that you would not, as was the case with the Speaker in ancient times, often acting as the agent of the King, force the House of Commons to vote supply before the grievances of a fellow Canadian were redressed.
I wish, this evening, Mr. Speaker, to present the case of a fellow Canadian. I do not know him personally, but I do know that he is a brother of a gentleman who for years was a member of the House; I refer to Mr. Burnham, former representative for the county of Peterborough. It is as a fellow-Canadian that I present Dr. Burnham's grievance to my right hon. friend the leader of the House of Commons and to the country.
First of all, who is Dr. Burnham? I am informed that he is a graduate of Manitoba University; that he was for years a distinguished medical practitioner in the city of Winnipeg; that he was a brilliant surgeon, and that he has published books bearing upon the line of work which he has pursued, books which are well known in the scientific world. When in 1914 the

Great War was declared Dr. Burnham happened to be on the ocean on a trip round the world. True to his traditions and to his love of the Mother Land, Dr. Burnham immediately decided that he should serve in the ranks. Accordingly, he interrupted his trip and boarded a ship at San Francisco-
