I believe it was the Ortiga. I may mention in passing, that after proceeding some distance the Ortiga was chased for several days by the famous German raider Emden. However, he landed in Europe, offered his services to the Allies, and being a surgeon and most anxious to give his services, as did our gallant friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) in Belgium, in hospital work, he was assigned to a hospital in Montenegro at a place called Plevna. Not long afterwards, as war was raging most intensely in that district, he was with thousands of others driven from Montenegro in the great Serbian retreat, where thousands were lost and he himself nearly perished. He managed, however, to escape and subsequently served continuously during a year on the Western front. Then he was sent to Salonika and there put in charge of a relief hospital, in which post he remained until 1919, giving most excellent service. In that year, being somewhat exhausted and his health failing, he returned to Canada on leave of absence, and proceeded to his home in Winnipeg. I may say that for his gallant service on the batlefield and in the hospitals and relief missions he received several decorations. Having returned to Winnipeg, where he had a host of friends, he started to organize a Canadian war hospital. He had seen with his own eyes the desperate situation to which the Serbians, the Montenegrins and the Albanians had been reduced and he knew by experience what efficient service could be rendered if a Canadian war hospital could be organized. His efforts met with a great measure of success. Not only did the citizens of Winnipeg subscribe large sums of money to the object, but municipalities in Manitoba and in other western provinces contributed generously. In 1919 he again left for Serbia and Montenegro, and made his headquarters at a place called Dulcigno. He was in charge of relief work there for several months until his activities were interrupted by the Serbian authorities.
I do not intend to read all the letters written by Dr. Burnham or the controversial letters exchanged between the Serbian consul and Dr. Burnham's friends. I will simply recite the grounds of complaint which have been urged by Dr. Burnham

himself, and the House will judge whether under such circumstances the Government is not justified in taking action in order that the grievances of Dr. Burnham may be redressed. In a letter dated December 13, 1920, Dr. Burnham states as follows his grounds of complaint against the Serbian administration:
As officer-in-command of the White Cross Mission-
It is a Canadian organization.
-I have to complain of the Serbian administration as follows:	,
(1)	That the Mission was under constant
police surveillance.	*
That is Serbian police surveillance.
(2)	That without known reason, two nurses were ordered to appear before the authorities at Antivari. Bearing in mind the painful experience elsewhere described the order was ignored.
(3)	That the Serbian authorities sent and order coupled with a police threat, to open the White Cross magazine for examination.
(4)	That in my absence, members of the staff were ordered before the Serbian authorities and terrorized.
(5)	That they seized material shipped into the country for the relief of the inhabitants, that the cases were opened and when released did not contain the quantities cited in the'invoices.
I may say that this material had been shipped largely from Canada, consisting of contributions from Canadians.
(6)	That they seized the boat whereby material was conveyed from steamer to port, and that although the boat had been leased from the owner, the White Cross never afterwards had the use of it.
(7)	That I was ordered before the Serbian Government at Antivari who made threats against the Mission and stated that it was no longer safe to remain in Montenegro.
(8)	That shortly after the Serbian Governor came to Dulcigno and again summoned me. In the interview which followed Lekitch repeated former threats and concluded by ordering the Mission out of the country. On being requested to put the order in writing he refused.
(9)	That on August 17, while waiting for the departure of the steamer at Antivari I was arrested by order of the Serbian Governor in the presence of one hunderd people on the quay, and
(10)	That I was sent under guard of a soldier with rifle and bayonet to the Hotel Marina where I was detained four hours.
(11)	That in consequence of the foregoing I was compelled to return on foot to Dulcigno where I arrived after midnight in an exhausted condition, having walked fifty-twTo miles during the day with the thermometer standing at 85 f. at midnight.
(12)	That on the departure of the White Cross Mission for Albania, the Serbian authorities refused to allow the transfer of the stores and material belonging to the Mission.
He states in the same letter:
I have compiled accurate case reports of people in the number of 2,152 who availed themselves of the medical services alone. No further evidence is necessary to show that no reliance whatsoever can be placed in the statements emanating from the Serbian Government respecting affairs in Montenegro.
The letter is signed:
F. W. E. Burnham.
Sir, I am not concerned with political agitation which may exist in Serbia and Montenegro; I am not concerned at all with the quarrels which are too evident between the two above-named countries; but one must not forget that the Dominion of Canada was an ally of both Montenegro and Serbia from the beginning until the end of the war. There is, it seems to me -and it is a fact indeed-in the comity of nations, even as between enemies on the battlefield, a protection for Red Cross and such like. A fortiori is there a protection as between allies fighting and dying for the same cause? We have been told repeatedly, during this session and, indeed, during the last few years, that Canada is a nation. Not later than two or three weeks ago, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) was defining what the new Act meant in speaking of a Canadian national, we were told that Canada was a nation; that before long, as soon as it pleased Canada, she might have consular representation, even an ambassador in the neighbouring republic. I should like to test this evening the statement made by one prominent member of the Government and know from the leader of the House (Mr. Meighen) if Canada is really a nation. There is one statement which certainly cannot be discounted-Canada is a member of the League of Nations and, therefore, Canada, whether a nation or not, but a member of the League of Nations, is certainly concerned with her nationals, not only at home, but especially abroad. Even if Canada were not a full-fledged nation, shall I be told that this Dominion, the premier Dominion of the British Empire, my native land, will stand for the humiliations, outrages and indignities inflicted on Canadian nurses and a Canadian surgeon doing work to serve a humanitarian cause, and that under the flag of one of her Allies?
I have to take exception to the statements which have been made by the Serbian consul against Dr. Burnham. He has written to several newspapers denying the statements made by Dr. Burnham, and even accusing him of political intrigue in the performance of his duties in Montenegro.



Mr. Speaker, I resent the insults of a foreigner, even though he be a consul, against i fellow-Canadian of the standing of Dr. Burnham, who, to serve the cause of humanity, to relieve the sick, the poor, and the oppressed in those distant lands, left everything behind him and consecrated his life and his talents to that purpose. I say that the least the Government should do is to ask the Serbian authorities to recall their consul who has libelled in the press the good name and the good faith of Dr. Burnham.
Another point I wish to emphasize is that until an investigation has taken place, and until the statements of Dr. Burnham which I have just quoted have been proven false, and, if sustained, until an apology and reparations have been made, the Government of this country, through the League of Nations, should prevent any Red Cross funds coming from Canada or the British Empire from being apportioned in favour of Serbia. To give you, Mr. Speaker, an idea of the spirit which animated Dr. Burnham let me read the last sentence of one of his letters:
Thus we close the first chapter of the activities of the Canadian White Cross in the Balkans. We look back without regrets. To retrace our steps would be to .do exactly the same. We throw in our lot with the poor, the sick and the oppressed. It was for them that this fund was organized. We resolutely set our face against injustice in every form. To have chosen differently would have been easier, but would not have been the policy of the White Cross or in harmony with the spirit of the people of Canada.
You have in that sentence the ring of honesty, and I ask that the Government investigate the complaints which I have just recited-that Canadian nurses were terrorized, that the materials sent from Canada were seized, that the surgeon and his staff were prevented from continuing their work amongst the poor and the sick, and that finally they were all ejected from the country. I say it isAhe duty of the Canadian Government to investigate this case and to see that justice is done.
I do not wish to be more historical than necessary, but let me recall to my right hon. friend the leader of the House a case which in many respects, is parallel to the one I have just mentioned. I refer to the Don Pacifico case when Lord Palmerston, then Minister of Foreign Affairs, despatched the British fleet to the Piraeus' in order that-the Greek government might compensate Don Pacifico for the losses sustained. It was stated at the time that Don Pacifico had very poor antecedents, TMr. Lemieux.]
that he was British, but of foreign origin, and that he had fyled a very extravagant claim arising out of the riots which had taken place in Athens, the capital of Greece. Here is the answer of Lord Palmerston:
The rights of a man depend on the merits of the particular case; and it is an abuse of argument to say that you are not to give redress to a man because in some former transactions he may have done something which is questionable. Punish him, If you will-punish him if he is guilty, but don't pursue him as a pariah through life. . . . "Oh, but," it is said "what an ungenerous proceeding to employ so large a force against so small a power!" Does the smallness of a country justify the magnitude of its evil acts? Is it to be held that if your subjects suffer violence, outrage, and plunder-
That is the case in the present instance.
-in a country which is small and weak, you are to tell them, when they apply for compensation, that the country is so weak and small, that we cannot ask it for compensation? Their answer would be that the weakness and smallness of the country makes it the more easy to obtain redress.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me repeat the question I put a moment ago: Is Canada a nation? I say that if she is not a fully-fledged nation, she has at least acquired certain titles of nobility during the last great war. She is the premier Dominion of the British Empire, and if we cannot as a Dominion within the four corners of the British North America Act assert our rights and protect our nationals abroad, we still have the old British flag, which protects every British subject wherever he is to be found in the four quarters of the globe. I should like to quote what Lord Palmerston said in the case of Don Pacifico in perhaps the most eloquent speech of his life. In his famous peroration he says:
I therefore fearlessly challenge the verdict which this House, as representing a political, a commercial, a constitutional country, is to give on the question before it; whether the principles on which the foreign policy of this country has been conducted, and the sense of duty which has led us to think ourselves bound to afford protection to our fellow subjects abroad, are proper and fitting guides for those who are charged with the government of England, and whether, as the Roman in the days of old held himself free from indignity when he could say Civis Bomanus sum, so also a British subject, in whatever land he be, shall feel confident that the watchful eye and the strong arm of England shall protect him against injustice and wrong.
I repeat, Sir, that if the Canadian Government feel that they have not the power to redress the legitimate grievances of Dr. Burnham and the noble nurses who were subjected to such humiliation and indignities at the hands of Serbian officials, they

should draw the attention of the Foreign Office in London to the matter, and, through that channel, obtain justice for these British subjects. It was my privilege some years ago to be in the city of Rome. It was in the year 1909, and on that occasion I witnessed some very grave riots that took place in the Eternal City. These incidents occurred after the execution in Spain of a Spaniard named Ferrer, and the anarchists of Europe being of the opinion that this act was unwarranted and that the governments of the Continent should rise up in arms against the government of Spain. In many of the cities on the Continent, in Paris and in Rome, the Spanish Embassy had to be guarded not only by the police, but also by the military authorities. In Rome, the anarchists for a few days seemed to hold sway; there were general strikes, and riot after riot raged in that great city. I happened one day to visit the Superior of the Canadian College in Rome on a well known thoroughfare, the street of the Four Fountains. That college is under the jurisdiction of the Sulpician Fathers, who, as the House knows, are amongst the oldest French religious orders, together with the Jesuits and the Recollets, to have done missionary and educational work in this country. That institution in which our young men pursued their theological studies is under the direction of the Sulpician Fathers. In that year the Superior was a distinguished Canadian from St. Hyacinthe. The Canadian College is not far from the Spanish Embassy, and was consequently very much exposed to the anarchists and rioters who were passing back and forth in the vicinity. I asked the Superior whether he was not a little too exposed and did not fear for the young priests and students who were under his charge. He pointed to the British flag and replied: "With that flag flying I fear nothing." Sir, it seems to me that under the protection of the British flag, as was so eloquently said by Lord Palmerston, Dr. Burnham, whom I do not know, and who has no other claim upon me than the fact that he is a fellow Canadian, should receive justice. His staff of devoted nurses who were subjected to persecution at the hands of the Serbian Government should also be accorded, through the instrumentality of this Government, the protection which is the right of every British subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COMPLAINT OF DR. BURNHAM AGAINST SIBERIAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The motion of the hon. member
as it appears on the Order Paper calls merely for the production of certain documents, being correspondence exchanged between the Canadian Government and the Serbian Government concerning the expulsion of Dr. Burnham and his hospital mission from Montenegro. Of course, to the production of the correspondence no objection can be made. But the hon. member in his address has assumed that the treatment of Dr. Burnham by the authorities in Montenegro, or in greater Serbia, has been such as to cast upon the Canadian Government the obligation of calling for atonement or redress, either through the Foreign Office or on our own initiative, from the offending government. I did not put myself in a position to argue, in view of the way the resolution reads, whether the presumption upon which the hon. member has based most of his address is correct or not.
Speaking from recollection, without having recently brought my mind to the facts, I am aware that some correspondence has taken place, and I believe that the Foreign Office has been consulted with regard to Dr. Burnham's complaint concerning his treatment in Montenegro. If I recollect rightly, Dr. Burnham came back to Canada, having already conducted some work in Montenegro in the earlier years of the war. I thought his return was earlier than the hon. gentleman mentioned; I was under the impression it was about 1917. So far as the Government was concerned, its only connection with him was to assist him in securing reduced passage back to carry on again the work in which he was interested there. Montenegro, it seems, is to be, subject to certain delimitations, a part of Greater Serbia. Within the confines of Montenegro a party has arisen whose purpose is to resist its incorporation in Greater Serbia, and who carry on there a political agitation, if indeed they do not go farther, in order to make effective that resistance. Dr. Burnham's troubles are claimed to have arisen from the fact that he espoused the cause of the minority in Montenegro and became involved in political agitation there. Whether that is true or not, I should not like finally to say; but, at all events, troubles have arisen in connection with him and correspondence has taken place. If that correspondence, when brought down, discloses that there has been any failure or default on the part of the Government in looking into the merits of the complaint made, or in seeking redress if the merits of the complaint are

established, then, of course, it will be time enough for the House to take action.
I was intensely interested in the address of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), and, what is more, I was exceedingly pleased, not only with its substance but with the enthusiasm with which the doctrines propounded by the hon. gentleman were set forth. The hon. member asked me, as head of the Government, to say whether or not this country is a nation, and, if it is, whether or not it purposes to assert the attributes and rights of a nation in respect of the claims of one of its citizens wronged in far away Montenegro. Well, I have no hesitation or doubt at all in answering the question. Canada unquestionably is a nation, and something more than a nation. It enjoys a status and rights in the world beyond those which other nations of its strength and age enjoy. Canada is as well, a member of the great British Commonwealth of Nations, and as such is in the position to assert such authority as its own strength, and moral status entitle it to assert; but, also, the authority of the Motherland and of that entire League of Nations known as the British Empire, if their concurrence in our position is obtained.
It was, however, interesting indeed to hear this position taken up and espoused by the hon. member for Maisonneuve, a member of the Liberal party in Canada; and particularly interesting was it to hear him refer to that famous debate in the British Parliament on the Don Paeifico claims, to hear him quote from the speech of Lord Palmerston, and point to the doctrine which that speech contained as the proper motto for Canada to adopt in her march among the nations of the world. I remember reading that speech. It has been referred to time and again, not only in this country but in general literature, as expressive of the extremely Imperialistic attitude of the British Tory, as jingoism of the highest type. And I recall at the moment the reply of Mr. Gladstone, delivered early in the morning after Lord Palmerston had spoken, in which the old statesman described the speech to which he had listened; in which he described the spirit that it embodied; in which he said that this high and mighty Imperialistic attitude which Lord Palmerston had assumed, was typical of the old Roman statemanship, and was expressed in those lines of the poet:
Oh Rome 'twas thine alas with awful sway To rule mankind and make the world ohey,
Disposing peace and war thine own majestic way.

Whatever may have been the rights of Don Paeifico, it was claimed to be doubtful at the time whether they were great enough, or fundamentally strong enough, to warrant the intervention of the British Fleet. But if the example of the British Government in the Don Paeifico case is to be followed by Canada, it undoubtedly can only be followed if this country maintains not only the name but the attributes of a nation- unless, in a word, we maintain that strength behind the word of Canada which will enable us to speak with substantial authority. I commend the address of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, I commend the doctrine that he has espoused tonight, I commend the spirit with respect to the mission of this country which evidently animates him, to all hon. gentlemen around and behind him, and especially to his leader who, only a few months ago, moved in this House that we should strip ourselves of naval and military strength and leave ourselves powerless. The mere word of any country does not go very far without any strength behind it.
Now the hon. gentleman-on the assumption again that a wrong has been done a Canadian citizen, a wrong that the courts and civil authorities of the State that is supposed to have done it have refused to redress-asks us to invoke not only the power of the Foreign Office, not only any authority that Canada may exert of herself, but, as well, to invoke the influence of the League of Nations, and if need be to see to it that any moneys that might come to Serbia from the reparation that Germany is required to make are withheld from Serbia pending atonement for the wrongs done by her to Dr. Burnham.

speechtext:
I thought the hon. gentleman spoke of "reparation funds," anyway he suggested that moneys be withheld from Serbia. I am not apprehensive that it will be necessary to go to that length. In fact I have not yet been convinced-I have not the papers before me because I did not know that the hon. member intended to do more than move his resolution-that wrong has been done. I do not think, at least, that there is information now in the Department of External Affairs to warrant the Government in assuming that there is cause for specific intervention. If the papers disclose that there has been cause, and that intervention has not taken place, then, of course, the time will come for Parliament

to speak its mind. I am not convinced that the papers will disclose such cause, nor am I sure that the papers will not disclose quite the opposite. However if it be found that there is something in the complaint that Dr. Burnham has made, and which the hon. member to-night has pressed on the floor of Parliament, then it may be altogether proper that we should invoke the assistance of the Foreign Office and it should be possible to secure such redress as will be appropriate to the wrong done. I do not think the matter will need to go to the length indicated in my hon. friend's address. Let me repeat that the subject has not been neglected; I know that communications have passed; I know that some information has been obtained; and I think it will be found that there has been nothing in the way of neglect on the part of the Department of External Affairs.

subtopic: COMPLAINT OF DR. BURNHAM AGAINST SIBERIAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Before this debate closes I would like to add a word in support of the statement of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve. The facts in connection with this case were, I think, first brought to the attention of the Canadian public by Mr. Arthur G. Penny, the Editor of the Quebec Chronicle. I may say for the information of the House, Mr. Speaker, that the Chronicle is not a newspaper which could by any manner of means, be accused of having tendencies other than those of the most orthodox Conservative kind. For a considerable period the Quebec Chronicle carried on an agitation, if I might so term it, on behalf of Dr. Burnham, and on reading its article we come to the conclusion that in so far as we are able to obtain confirmation of the facts placed before us, Dr. Burnham a Canadian citizen, a colonel in the Canadian or the Imperial army, and a brother of an ex-member of this House, whilst carrying on a work of mercy in a foreign country was subjected to certain outrages and indignities. It would appear from his statements-and they have not as yet been contradicted, though more than six months have elapsed since they were first made to the Canadian people-that our fellow countrymen and women were terrorized by some petty Balkan bureaucrat, that goods and money sent by Canadian citizens to help the starving, the oppressed and the miserable in Europe were taken and used for other purposes, and that finally one of our own ex-soldiers, a man who bears a high reputation in Canada was forcibly ejected from Serbia. His mission was backed by the funds of individual citizens ,of Western Canada, by municipalities throughout the Dominion and even by provincial governments, and moreover Dr. Burnham went overseas, if not with the authorization of the Dominion Government, at least, as admitted by the Prime Minister, with its knowledge and consent. The only answer we get when the matter is brought on the floor 9 p.m. of the House is that some time, sooner or later, we may obtain
redress.
Perhaps I am one of those who have placed too literal an interpretation on the language used in this House and outside by hon. gentlemen who have represented us both at the Imperial conferences and at the meetings of the League of Nations when they said that we were a nation, for when they said that I thought they meant we had the attributes of a nation and that our citizens were not to be insulted with impunity by any petty sovereign or bureaucrat. I understood, as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said, that we were more than a nation-though I am not quite prepared to be so enthusiastic as he about the reason why we are more than a nation. He stated we were so because we belonged to the Great Britannic commonwealth, and being backed as we were by this grat commonwealth we would not have the slightest difficulty in having our rights and privileges respected by other nations. The history of our boundary relations with the United States has not given me any great confidence in the value which my right hon. friend places in this alliance. However, taking his word for it that we have increased the value of our nationhood by such an alliance, and by recent events in Europe and elsewhere, I cannot understand how it comes about that we must wait for months and months until some petty clerk in the British foreign office decides that probably one Canadian might have been insulted by a ruler of one of the Balkan States. It seems to me that it is the duty of the Canadian Government and the Canadian people to protect our citizens where-ever they may be.
Although I do not join in the enthusiasm of my right hon. friend from Maisonneuve and Gaspe with regard to the words used by Lord Palmerston in the Don Pacifico debate, and although I do not agree that we should go about the world with a chip on our shoulder blustering about our rights and our powers and shouting Civis Britannicus sum, I do believe that if we are to place any value on our citizenship we should

have the means of being able to protect our nationals. I do not think anyone in this House would ask the Government to declare war on Serbia, for there are other measures which can be taken, financial and economic, and strong diplomatic pressure could be brought to bear. Then, as my hon. friend from Gaspe said, there is the League of Nations. That League, I understood was formed for the protection of the small as well as the great nations. How well these small nations have been protected would be a question perhaps for further discussion. For instance, how well the doctrine of self determination has been upheld in the case of this same little country of Montenegro would be a question which the League of Nations might very well ponder.
However, this is the point which I think should be taken up by this House. If a British subject is proud of being able to say he is a British subject in whatever part of the world he may be, and if being a British subject implies protection in every way, so should the title of being a Canadian national. I would not say, like my hon. friend from Gaspe, Civis Britanni-cus sum; I would say Civis Canadensis sum. Our men have made Canada so well known in the world that she is no longer a stranger. And I would ask that the Government make such representations as would lead the world to understand that our nationals cannot be insulted and outraged with impunity, however far they may be from their native land.

subtopic: COMPLAINT OF DR. BURNHAM AGAINST SIBERIAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). The hon. and gallant gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Power) I think rather assumed to send our fleet into the Adriatic. I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Maisonneuve with great interest, and he certainly spoke temperately and with dignity. I think we should first do what he asks for, that is, investigate the charges. He did not state that the charges were true, he simply asked the Government to take measures to investigate them. In that he is entirely right. All I can say is, if those charges are true, it is a case of base ingratitude on the part of Serbia, because this young nation plunged into the war with the greatest courage and chivalry to uphold, among other things, the rights of small nations, and particularly the rights of Serbia, who was the first pation to get us embroiled in the war.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, although I am not a swashbuckling imperialist and though I do not go round, as the hon. and gallant gentleman said, with a chip on my shoulder, I think we may rely upon the right hon. gentleman who is the head of the Government in this country, if he discovers that injustice has been done to a Canadian citizen, to be the first to uphold the cause of the nation with that dignity and firmness which are characteristic of him. It is a very good occasion upon which to let the whole world know that the rights of Canadian citizens must be respected everywhere. The Government should take every step necessary to the fullest investigation of this matter and adopt such measures as the facts seem to warrant.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the seconder of the motion I feel that I should like to say a word or two on the subject. I am not quite satisfied with the enthusiasm, if it could be called enthusiasm at all, with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) dealt with this motion. We should all be of one mind in regard to the matter brought to our attention by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). We have to accept the word of a British subject until conclusive evidence to the contrary is presented to the House or to some tribunal inquiring into the matter. A British subject has made certain statements; they are presented to the House by the hon. member for Maisonneuve, and I for one accept for the time being those statements as being correct. If they are correct, they certainly require a most thorough investigation and it is for the Canadian people, both on their own behalf and as part of the great British Empire, to give Montenegro or any other country strictly to understand that Canadian subjects are not to be treated unfairly with impunity.
Now, the answer that we received from the Prime Minister to this motion is a fling at the Liberal party, an attempt to belittle the Liberal party and to tell us some things that we ought to know if we have such big notions concerning ourselves as British subjects or as Canadians or as members of this Parliament. I did not think, Sir, that there was any possible way by which the right hon. gentleman could get around to that attitude in connection with this motion. As the hon. member for Skag-way has said-

speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) will pardon me for not remembering for the moment the name of the constituency which he graces and honours, as he does the whole of Canada. I thought that the case was presented with fullness, with dignity, in a manner quite free from the slightest degree of political bias. But my right hon. friend says it would be well for the hon. member who proposes the motion to look around him and see what sympathy he is getting from his own side of the House; that it would be well for him to inquire into the history of the Liberal party and see what they have done to make Canada a nation or to maintain her in that position. Well, I would ask the right hon. gentleman where the party to which he belongs stood in 1882 when we were called upon as an integral part of the Empire to send troops to the Soudan, where they were much needed. Wh'at was the answer of Sir John A. Macdonald? "Not a dollar, not a ship, not a man; let England fight her own battles; we have nothing to do with them." That was the answer of Sir John A. Macdonald, and not a man was sent; a few Canadian voyageurs went on their own responsibility. That was the attitude of the Conservative party in 1882 when it was at the zenith of its glory and headed by the biggest statesman it ever had.
What was the attitude of the Liberal party when the South African war broke out? That was the second opportunity which this country had to show what it wanted to do as a part of the British Empire. I need not recite to you, Sir, the attitude that was taken by that great statesman, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was at the head of the Liberal Government at that time. Instead of saying to the British Empire: "Not a man, not a dollar! Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: "The last man, the last dollar; everything that we can do to support the Empire in this crisis." That was the first great step taken by Canada along the lines that we are now discussing, the first great event in connection with which Canada was brought prominently in contact with the affairs of the world. And is my right hon. friend to tell us that we should look around; that we should examine our history and see what our antecedents have been as citizens of Canada and as subjects of the British Empire? Speaking for myself, I take no slurs from the right hon. gentleman as to my relationship with the
British Empire or the British flag. I am just as strong in that regard as he is, and that is true of everybody connected with my family during the last two or three hundred years. I therefore do not take kindly to anything coming even from the Prime Minister which tends to reflect in the slightest degree upon the attitude of the Liberal party in this respect.
About the time when I came to this Parliament, in 1904, a case occurred which was somewhat analagous to this. A small sailing schooner, having on board some natives of Nova Scotia, had been improperly seized at a port of Uruguay; the vessel was confiscated, and the men lost their furs and their money. The first word that I said publicly in this House was to ask Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government to look after the interests of those men away down in Uruguay with their schooner and their furs confiscated. What happened? The government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier appointed a commissioner, conferred proper powers upon him, and sent him to Uruguay. A full investigation was made, and he returned and reported conditions to the then government. The Republic of Uruguay was obliged, through the British consul there, to make compensation for the schooner and the furs which they had confiscated. There was a case in which we did something along those lines. There was no hesitation about the matter; there was no speech-making on the part of the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier; his government immediately went to work and redressed the grievances of those men.	.
All that we are asking for in this case is that proper steps should be taken; that we should not be governed by the correspondence that has reached us from Serbia. That correspondence is tainted and coloured to suit the views of the people of that country. I would not be satisfied with this correspondence. I presume they have a consul in Great Britain, and Great Britain has consuls in that country. If this matter cannot be handled through Canadian avenues, the British consul in that country should be called upon to inquire into the matter and report, and in that way we can get at the facts without the high colouring that may be given to them through this correspondence. The Prime Minister should make a more pronounced deliverance on that point, and not say that he is simply going to wait; that he will give another reading to this correspondence, and that if he is convinced by the correspondence that has been received from the defendant in

this case, he may do something to redress the grievances of Dr. Burnham. I am not quite satisfied with that. I think a little stronger statement should be given, so that Canadians, wherever they may be, may realize to the full that they have behind them at home a people, a Parliament and a Government always keenly on the lookout to see that they are properly safeguarded and protected in both their persons and their property.

I wish to thank hon.
gentlemen on both sides of the House who have supported the principle involved in this motion, and I hope that means will be taken to hold an investigation to find out whether or not the grievances of Dr. Burnham and his nurses are really deserving of our attention, as I have no doubt they are.
Before taking my seat, I wish to tell the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that he is quite in error if he believes that I am animated by any jingo spirit in proclaiming "Civis Britannicus sum." If my hon. friend will read my remarks in Hansard to-morrow, he will see that I have said .that, if Canada is really a nation, she can, through her own channels, obtain redress in the present instance, but if there is no possibility, as we have no foreign office or foreign minister ourselves, of Canada obtaining justice for one of her nationals, John Bull is always at the old stand and, as for one hundred and fifty years we have lived under the British flag, we may still invoke the protection of that flag so that one of our fellow-Canadians may be protected against any humiliation, indignity or outrage abroad. That is what I said. It is true that we have in Canada the Department of External Affairs, of which I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) is the minister, ex-officio. If my right hon. friend will take this matter in hand, will investigate it and see that justice is done, as I have no doubt he will if he has that authority, I shall be the first one to proclaim that Canada is really a nation, or at least on the way to become a nation. But, meanwhile, if it is impossible, through that channel, 
through that machinery, to obtain justice for one of our nationals, I look to the British Foreign Office to redress the grievance of one of our citizens. By doing this I am not parading in the highways and byways with a chip on my shoulder; I am simply talking common sense and speaking the language of a good Canadian.
