speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. SEXSMITH (East Peterborough) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in order to give each voter an equal share in the representation, some system of proportional representation should be adopted, and that a special committee of this House should be forthwith appointed, charged with an enquiry into the different systems of proportional representation, with a view to recommend one of these for adoption.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting this resolution to the House, I do so with considerable timidity, because I realize there are, perhaps, members as well as many other people who look upon proportional representation as something new or somewhat of a fad. I would say to any one who may hold those ideas that it is not new and that to-day every country in the world, that has responsible government and an electoral system such as we have in Canada, is seriously discussing proportional

representation. I sincerely hope that something may be done in order that we may secure in Canada a better electoral system than we have at present. I trust this subject, that has to do with the national interest and that is something of much greater importance than the success of any party, may be freely and fully discussed from an unbiased and non-partisan standpoint.
The chief evil of our present system is that large and important sections of opinion are left unrepresented, and the end of all political reform should be to secure to these important sections their due and fair share of representation in this House. In speaking of the single member mode of representation, I do not think I can do better than quote from one of the most outstanding statesmen in Great Britain to-day, the Right Hon. Arthur James Balfour. Speaking before the Scottish Conservative Club, in Scotland, he said:
Everybody who has watched the actual course of a contested election in a constituency where parties were evenly balanced knows perfectly well the monstrous power which is given to a very small minority to exact a pledge from the candidate, not that he should support this or that great policy, but that he should help their small and particular interest.
I know of nothing which is more corrupting both to the electors or to the elected than that process, and, although I have fully seen the difficulties which attach to what is commonly known as minority representation, it surely is an extraordinary criticism upon our existing system that, while a small handful of interested people, can turn an election one way or the other on their own personal issue, huge minorities like the minority of the Unionists in Scotland are utterly and grossly unrepresented. We give every privilege to the little knot of people in the individual constituencies: we ignore the great mass who under our existing system 'find no representation at all comparable either to their numerical strength or their public spirit or to any other quality which makes them useful, able and independent citizens.
Those are very strong words from one who I am sure every hon. member of this House will regard as a great authority. I look upon his words as a very strong condemnation of our present single member electoral system
Looking over our election returns in this country, I find that we have large majorities grossly unrepresented in this country. I should like, if time permitted, to go over all the provinces of Canada and give to the House the results of elections during the last decade or two under our present system. In the province of Quebec, for instance, in the general election of 1900, fifty-seven Liberals and eight Conservatives were
elected. The fifty-seven Liberals secured 133,566 votes, and the eight conservatives 103,253. The average number of votes required to elect one Conservative was 12,907, while the average number of votes to elect one Liberal was 2,344. Thus one Liberal vote had the value of six Conservative votes. Under proportional representation thirty-seven Liberals would have been elected instead of fifty-seven and twenty-eight Conservatives instead of eight.
Take the election of 1904 in the same great province. Then fifty-four Liberals were elected, and eleven Conservatives. The fifty-four Liberals secured 144,992 votes, and the eleven Conservatives 111,550. The average number of votes required to elect one Liberal was 2,636, and the average number of votes required to elect one Conservative was 10,141. A Liberal vote had the value of four Conservative votes. Under proportional representation thirty-nine Liberals would have been elected instead of fifty-four and twenty-six Conservatives instead of eleven.
In that same election of 1904 we find that in the province of Nova Scotia 56,526 Liberal votes were cast and eighteen Liberal members elected, and that 46,131 Conservative votes were cast, but not one member was elected. In the same year practically the same condition obtained in the province of British Columbia.
In 1908 in the province of Quebec we find the results were very similar. The Liberals secured. 162,176 votes and elected p4 members, while the Conservatives secured 115,579 votes and elected 11 members. The average number of votes required to elect one Liberal was 3,003, and the average number of votes required to elect one Conservative was 10,144. One Liberal vote had the value of 3 Conservative votes. Under proportional representation 38 Liberals would have been elected instead of 54 and 27 Conservatives instead of 11.
These examples should be enough to convince any man in this House that any electoral system that allows such a condition to prevail where it is impossible to elect a Parliament that will properly reflect the opinion of all the people, which is one of the main principles of responsible Government, cannot possibly make for the welfare of our country, and I believe it is the duty of this Parliament, which is about to make a new redistribution of seats, to see that such a condition should



no longer prevail. Should we fail to improve it, in my opinion, this Parliament will have failed to do its duty towards the people.
If we look over conditions in other countries we find them very similar where the same electoral system prevails, and in passing I may say that every country in the world that has responsible government has practically the same electoral system of single member constituencies. We find in Great Britain in the general election of 1874, and these are the reasons, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Balfour and many other British statesman are looking very seriously at the present system, which is absolutely unfair, the Conservatives had a majority of 50 in Parliament although the Liberal vote polled was 1,400,000, against a total Conservative vote of 1,200,000. In other words, although the Liberals in that election polled 200,000 more votes than the Conservatives, the Conservatives having a majority of 50 in the House, the Parliament of that great country was elected and served on a minority vote.
Again, in the British election of 1906, the ministerialist group had 56 per cent of the votes polled and elected 72 per cent of the members, while the Conservatives had 44 per cent of the votes polled and elected 28 per cent of the members. The unprecedented ministerial majority of 256 should have been the safe majority of 68.
I have selected only a few outstanding cases but I could give many further examples if time permitted. In the United States in the Oregon election in 1896, the Republicans, with 55 per cent of the votes, elected 83 members to the Legislature, while the Democrats, with 34 per cent of the votes, elected 7. It required 4,499 votes to elect one Democrat, and 619 votes to elect one Republican. The Socialists and Prohibitionists, with 11 per cent of the vote, were unrepresented. I have been unable to secure the returns for some of the other provinces of Canada, but I am told on pretty good authority that the present Government in British Columbia secured only 37 per cent of the vote polled.
We have an example in Toronto to-day of a Government carrying on with a very small minority vote. Now, in regard to the by-elections in East Elgin and West Peterborough, I have not a word to say about the men that represent these ridings. They are no doubt good representatives, but they failed to secure a majority of the total votes polled. Is it fair, or proper, or democratic that we should suffer to
[Mr. Sexsmith.}
exist an electoral system that allows such a condition of things? The principles of democratic government, by the people and for the people, are well established in the minds of citizens, but in my opinion they have failed jto work out in practice. For example, in the election of 1904, when the great question of building the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental railway was the main subject before the people of this country, what was the situation? That was the question on which the election was decided, and I think it is fair to assume that all those who voted Conservative at that time were opposed to that railway proposition. In the province of Quebec, under our electoral system, 54 supporters of the proposition were elected and only 11 opponents, whereas, under proportional representation, the respective figures would have been 39 supporters and 26 opponents. In other words, had the election of 1904 been conducted under the proportional system, Quebec would have elected 26 opponents to the proposition instead of 11, and 39 supporters instead of 54, or a difference of 15 supporters fewer and fifteen opponents more. In the good province of Nova Scotia, 46,000 electors did nqt secure one representative; they did not secure a voice in the House at all, although they had within 10,000 of half the vote. The Liberals elected 18 supporters and the Conservatives, who were at that time opposing the measure, failed to secure one representative. I am convinced that had the election been run under the proportional system, and had the people's minds been properly reflected in the House, that ill-advised and ill-considered railway proposition would never have been put through and Canada could have gone along and developed on safer and saner lines. '
Now, the spirit of democracy requires that an equal share of representation shall be given each separate elector, and not that the direction of government shall be entrusted exclusively to one class or party. The first duty of a democracy should be to respect the rights of its citizens. Ever since the earliest days of responsible goy- ' ernment, and you may go back centuries in the history of the great British nation, when the first representative government was formed, and follow it down to the present day, there has been a steady development until we have our present great system of government. But in the earlier times only a very small coterie of people had the franchise, and from those days

until now the masses have been clamouring for the extension of the franchise. Why did they want the franchise? It was because, in all those years, there was a feeling that the people did not rule, and they believed that if they had the vote they would have sufficient power to control government, and would really have democracy. The franchise has been extended until, at present, almost every adult in the great British Empire has the vote. Yet, notwithstanding this universal application of the principle, the people have been unable to control government sufficiently to see that the different elements of the nation have a fair and equal share in the councils of the country and, may I say particularly, in its inner councils.
A short time ago a thoughtful editorial appeared in the Ottawa Journal. It pointed out that from 1896 to the present day not one farmer from the great province of Ontario had ever been taken into the Cabinet; not one had ever been taken into the inner councils' of the nation. I ask, in all fairness and sincerity: Is there a man in this House who could say that in that great and important class in the province of Ontario one man could not have been found with sufficient ability to warrant his inclusion in the Cabinet? I say that there is not an honourable gentleman who would dare stand up on the floor of Parliament and so aver. Yet fifty per cent, we may say, of the people of the province of Ontario, so far as the inner councils of the nation have been concerned, have been disfranchised. Wonder has been expressed at the farmers organizing and going into politics. Well, Spencer says that self-preservation is the first law of nature, and I look to my right to-night and see there the nucleus of a farmers' party. I have heard that party variously called the Agrarian party and the Farmers' party, and there is not a man in this House who has more respect for the farmers or the agrarians, by whichever name you choose to call them, than I have. There is no man in this House who has fought the battles of the farmers longer and more strenuously than I have done, or who is more desirous to see them get their right and fair share in this country. But I must say that if the Farmers' party of to-day aims at becoming the sole governors of the country, then I cannot endorse any such ideal. If, in the past, the people from the urban centres have been governing, that is no reason or excuse for the farmers now to say that because they have perhaps a majority of votes, they will retaliate and elect a government to run the country, and that the people of the cities and towns will have to submit. No. This is a great country, stretching -from the Atlantic to the Pacific, with millions of farmers, and room for millions more, and millions of citizens in the great and glorious cities of Canada, of which we are all proud, and room for more; and if the Agrarian party desire to serve the best interests of the country, then, instead of seeking to become the governors of the country, they should be willing to join hands with others in the direction of affairs.
If I had my way, I would dispense with all parties, and that is not a conclusion which I have reached only to-day; it is probably some ten years since I saw the advisability of it. I would elect a Parliament of sensible Canadian citizens to come here and deal with the questions of the country on their merits, and not from any party standpoint or party bias; and for the farmers to come as a separate class and say: "We are going to make an effort, if possible, to seize the reins of power, and to govern the country," is an attitude which I cannot support. When a man elects to become the representative of one class he then, to my mind, ceases to be a representative and becomes a delegate. Professor John R. Commons, professor of political economy in the University of Wisconsin, has said "That one man of wealth has the influence of a thousand farmers, storekeepers and labourers." Well, with my experience I would be inclined to think that in some instances you might multiply his estimate a thousand fold.
We are living in a democratic age, an age, I trust, of advancement, but a time of unrest-even dangerous unrest-a time when people are dissatisfied with the old order of things. So many strange evils have sprung into life that one is bewildered. On the one hand we find unusual concentration of wealth in the control of a few; on the other, a growing restlessness and frantic attempts at organization on the part of the wage-earning class. I believe the Government should have an important place in solving these contradictions, and I believe that the remedy lies in the adoption of a proportional representation system in elections.
Let me quote what Lord Robert Cecil, an eminent man in public life in Great Britain, says. At a luncheon held in the House of Commons, London, England, on November 3, 1920, Lord Robert Cecil, speak-

ing on proportional representation, uttered the following words:
I am satisfieid, that propirtional representation has never been more important that it is at the present moment. We are faced all over the world by an attack on what may be called the world order,-a general challenge and dispute on the presupposition of which the whole of our civilization and society is based. It is a time when democracy as a system of government and as a system of social organization is going to be tested to its uttermost, and the machinery which expresses democracy will be overhauled by no friendly critics, to see whether it really does justify the claim it makes. In this country, we have for many years, been aware of a growing criticism of representative institutions as they actually exist. We know that some of our most cherished institutions no longer keep the position in the public reputation that they did half a century ago, and the additional danger exists now, that not only are there those who criticise our institutions, but there are those who desire definitely to set up a different form and method of governing the country which many of us, at any rate, think would lead us straight to anarchy.
It is a time when it boheves all of us who believe in democracy and in stability to look carefully at the foundations on which our institutions are based and to do our utmost to see that they really are based on the only foundation on which democratic institutions can be based, namely, a true accord with the expressed and determined will of the people. It is for that reason that, to my mind, proportional representation has an added importance at the present time.
At the same meeting Colonel L. S. Amery, Under Secretary of the Colonies said:
We are only beginning to realize-the general public I mean-that methods of election influence the whole character and structure of the political life. We have plenty of object lessons before us, both in the present and in the past. I was reading the other day the life of my first political chief, Lord Courtney, and I was impressed with the far-seeing grasp he showed, forty years ago, of the inevitable results of applying the old political system of election to the Irish problem-and he endorsed his belief by sacrificing his political position.
I believe that half, i-f not the whole of the appalling problem with which we are faced to-day is a by-product of an unfortunate system of elections which created artificial divisions and exaggerated them, when the important thing was for the men of moderate views to get together and find a real solution. If we had had proportional representation, forty years ago, a solution might have been found of the Irish problem then on the lines of moderate men of all shades of opinion, drawing together on common ground.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the different systems of proportional representation. That will be the work of the committee, if appointed. However, I may say I agree with Colonel L. S. Amery when he expresses the belief that, had proportional representation been
TMr. Sexsmith.]
adopted forty years ag'o ip the British Isles, a solution might have been found of the Irish problem. Our present system does not encourage unity of the Canadian people, which is so necessary for the well-being and general advancement of our country. It rather encourages the opposite. At election time we find Quebec talking about Orange Toronto, and Toronto talking about French Quebec, which, I think, does not make for unity. Does any man tell me that that mode of conducting elections is to the advantage of this country? Personally I cannot see it. In place of drawing our people closer together we, at election time, indulge in picayune methods in a constituency where a man can use " the glad hand " and resort to all the evils that may be attached to a corrupt election to try to secure his return. In a word the idea seems to be "Anything to get votes." We have to acknowledge these things because we all realize that they take place. Instead of talking in Montreal about Orange Toronto, and talking in Orange Toronto about French Quebec, we should, as some one has well said:
Be noble, and the nobleness
That lies in other men-sleeping but not dead-
Shall rise in majesty, to meet thine own.
There are many countries in Europe that have adopted proportional representation, and some countries in the British Empire where the system is in vogue. I do not deem it necessary to outline the conditions which exist in those countries, and the success which has followed the adoption of that system, but. I want to refer to a few cases in our own country where proportional representation has been tried. The system was tried in the city of Winnipeg a short time ago, during the Provincial election, and I now wish to quote the opinion of the Hon. Thomas H. Johnson, Attorney General of Manitoba, as to how it worked out.
Mr. Johnson wrote:
I feel I can truthfully say that I have not now, and never have had, a single regret for the efforts made by me, personally, in connection with the introduction of this reform in our election laws. The proportional representation system gives a more truly representative legislature than the system of single member constituencies. Everything claimed for it in the literature which we used, and with which we are familiar, was clearly accomplished. The electors of Winnipeg had no more difficulty than usual, and the counting, nothwithstanding the great number of candidates, forty-one in all), came off without a hitch of any kind.
I now wish to quote the opinion of another gentleman Mr. W. J. Tupper, K. C.,

a Conservative member of the Manitoba Legislature, who wrote:
In my opinion the test that proportional representation underwent in this city during the late provincial election, was successful. As I understand the system, it is intended to give representation to all parties in proportion to their numerical strength. The result of the late election showed that the minority parties in the city of Winnipeg received representation i-n accordance with their voting strength. It however, did not favour independent candidates, as you will have observed.
I may say that the success of the system seems to me to depend upon the effciency of those in control of the counting. We were fortunate in this province to have exceptionally able men in charge and 'the result is, no doubt, in a great measure due to them.	,
The mayor of Winnipeg, Mr. C. F. Gray, wrote:
I might say that I followed the application of this new system of election with keen interest and the results have satisfied me that it is the best means of ascertaining the wishes of all sections of the electorate. I look forward to its successful application in the forthcoming municipal election in the city of Winnipeg.
The Manitoba Free Press, in its issue of July 7, 1920, commented editorially on the election, as follows:
Winnipeg, it may be ventured, has put proportional representation upon a Canadian political map. The test the new system has successfully passed through in the recent Manitoba election is the last thing needed to demonstrate the practicability and merits of proportional representation. Its extension to the rural constituencies in Manitoba is assured, and its ultimate adoption of all elections-civic, provincial, and federal-may now be looked on as inevitable. In Winnipeg the test was classic, and proportional representation won with flying colors.
I have some other comments here which perhaps are worth puting on Hansard:
Some of the advantages of the new system are very apparent. In the first place, proportional representation eliminated the excitement and bitterness from the election campaign; the knowledge that each party could only get its fair proportion, and no more, of the available seats made the old-time stategy and electioneering useless-
That is worth considering, Mr, Speaker, if nothing more.
:-it also saves thousands of dollars which would have been spent in pushing individual candidates, and it enabled the electors to approach the ballots with a calmness of mind which gave them an opportunity to cast their votes with the greatest possible understanding and intelligence. The trifling number of spoiled ballots is an eloquent testimonial to the fact that the electors were cool and clear-headed when they went to the polls.
The leading fact, however, is that the result of the ballot has worked out with mathematical exactitude to the desired end ; the elected candidates represent in accurate proportion the
voting strength of the parties in the city; no votes were lost, and the voter who saw that his first choice had been defeated, knew that his vote was not extinguished, but passed on to his alternate preference, and that in the final results he had secured his correct proportion of representation.
I know there are those who think that proportional representation favours little cliques and independent candidates, but the results so far have proved the direct opposite.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after giving this question considerable thought I feel that something should be done to secure for this great country a better election system.
Last year we spent weeks of
10 p.m. valuable time trying to pass an election Act. Yes, we spent weeks trying to build barbed wire entanglements, if I may so express myself, around the polling booth so that the individual elector might be allowed to cast his vote without danger of its being switched or stolen. We acknowledge the principle of one man one vote, or one elector one vote, but we allow in our system of distribution the direct opposite. What would be thought of a government or of an individual member of this House that would introduce a bill giving the electors in one district six votes and those in the adjoining district one vote? What chance would a bill of that description have of adoption by this House? But that is exactly what has happened in some of our electoral districts, in every election for the last twenty years. In one district one Conservative vote might be worth five or siv Liberal votes; in another district that I have referred to in the province of Quebec, at one election, one Liberal vote was worth six Conservative votes; and in the province of Nova Scotia 46,000 Conservative votes out of a total of 103,000^-1 am speaking in round numbers- did not secure one representative in this chamber, while 56,000 Liberal votes elected eighteen representatives. While the Government of that day might have been elected by a small majority, still I look upon that as very significant because that is the year, 1904, when the great railway question which we are encumbered with to-day was before the country. There is not an hon. gentleman within sound of my voice who would hesitate for a minute in condemning any attempt that might be made to grant to our citizens in one district one vote and to those in another district five or six votes,

but that has been the result of our elections during the past year.
Say not it matters not to me My brother's weal is his behoof.
For in this wondrous human web If your life's warp, his life is woof.
Woven together are the threads And you and he are in one loom For good or ill, for sad or glad,
Tour lives must share one common doom. Then let the daily shuttle glide Wound full of threads of kindly care That life's great lengthening web may be Not only strongly wrought but fair.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us, is to my mind, well timed. The public is seriously considering this question and is intensely interested in it. It has received much study and is receiving more study. Such experience as we already have had in Canada with this system has been very satisfactory. I think the time for the introduction of the resolution is also well chosen because of what some people call the present political unrest, but which I prefer to call a political awakening.
People are doing their own thinking now as they have never done before in the world's history. There are extremists among labourers and among advanced thinkers, but we have always had extremists among thinking men and women. We must decide how we shall treat our extremists. In olden days they had a way of their own-those in authority adopted the plan of putting extremists to death as the handiest and most expeditious plan available; later on the plan of imprisonment was substituted; and in still later years Englishmen adopted the plan of allowing the extremist to shout himself hoarse in Hyde Park. The world mildly applauded- the heroic action of the Englishman, but hesitated about following his example. The world moves and the extremist is no longer satisfied with being allowed to air his view in the public parks. He wishes to be given the opportunity of expressing his views in the legislative halls of his country, and the idea is gradually gaining ground that where the extremist has any considerable backing he should have that opportunity, and that the only *safe course is to give it to him.
The best citizens are always drawn to

wards the under dog, and their sympathy always goes out to those who appear to be oppressed. They want to see every one have a chance, and the old plan of suppressing the extremist is no longer work-
able. The main result of suppressing the extremist was to get a new and bigger crop of his kind. We may kill or imprison the idealist, but we cannot kill or imprison the ideal. There is a law above the law of man and wiser than the law of man, which prevents that.
With education even so general as it is in our land, the only safe way is to give every encouragement to those having advanced thoughts to give expression to their thoughts, whether they be right or wrong. Public parks served their day as places for that expression, but to my mind election days and legislative halls are the proper times and places for their expression in our day. In the public parks there is no satisfactory method of answering the soap-box orator, but in this House all new ideas can be met under the most complete rules and regulations and in such a way that those new ideas will be subject to the acid test. They will be set before the public with their strength and their weakness clearly exposed to the public gaze. Each argument will be publicly met by those well qualified to meet it. All new ideas will be exposed to coldblooded public scrutiny, and I have sufficient faith in the public to believe that the general result will be that new ideas that are worth while will survive and in time will be put into effect, while those ideas not well founded will die. I doubt if there is any better place in Canada than this House in which to give effect to sound ideas and to kill unsound ideas. Carlyle, referring to the French Revolution, speaks of "truth clad in hell fire." It rests largely with this House to say how the new ideas of our day, be they true or false, shall come to us. It is largely ours to say whether they will come to us clothed in the garments of peace or dressed in the lurid garments described by Carlyle.
I do not think our extremists in any particular line are so numerous as some people suppose. They must be fairly numerous before they can get representation in this House even under the most democratic plan of proportional representation, but if extremists in any particular line are sufficiently numerous to obtain representation in the House under that plan, then I believe it is for the benefit of the country that they should come here and air their views in a place where those views can be properly met. Let me repeat that I believe if their views are well founded they will survive and eventually conquer, while if they are not well founded they will die.

This surely is as it should be. I believe vve should arrange that in all our cities, at least in those which are entitled to more than one representative, the constituencies should be grouped together and each elector should only have one first vote, being entitled to give second and further choices, where necessary, to other candidates. This would enable any group of people to obtain representation, provided they are sufficiently strong to be entitled to representation. In time, as the plan is worked out, it may be well to provide for the grouping together of a considerable portion of thickly peopled rural sections under the same plan. Possibly at present it might be well to try it out in cities where it can best be worked out, and in rural communities where we have only one member for each constituency we should have provision for a second choice where there are more than two candidates.
The hon. gentleman who moved this resolution has suggested that a committee should be appointed to go into the matter. That is certainly the proper course. There is no need of going into the details here or of elaborating any argument as to how the plan should be worked out. I have no doubt that a committee would be prepared to consider all phases of the question, not only the matter of proportional representation in grouped constituencies, if you like to use the term, but also the matter of transferable votes in single constituencies.
The hon. gentleman has said something with regard to the experiment in Manitoba. I suppose the House generally is aware that in the last local election in Manitoba provision was made for the working out of proportional representation in the city of Winnipeg. The city was granted ten representatives arid they were elected under proportional representation. In the country nothing of the kind was provided; no provision was made for transferable votes. Now, let us see how the different plans worked out. I refer again to the Free Press of July 5 last. The three groups which had any large representation in Winnipeg were Labour, Liberal and Conservative. Besides the candidates for these groups there were eleven Independent candidates, each representing, I suppose, some new idea of his own. The fear is sometimes expressed that some faddist or other might by means of this plan be elected to Parliament, but the Winnipeg experiment does not justify any idea of that kind. In Winnipeg, according to the Free Press figures, which, no doubt, are correct-they were published
some days after the election-the votes cast as first choice were 42.5 per cent Labour, 30.4 per cent Liberal, 13.7 per cent Conservative, and 13.4 per cent Independent. You will notice that the Independents had nearly as many votes as the Conservatives, but it must be remembered that the Conservative group was one group where as among the Independents there were anywhere from six to eleven groups, so to speak; there were eleven candidates. As a result of the voting, four Labour candidates, four Liberals and two Conservatives were elected. It might be said that only one Conservative and one Independent should have been elected, land perhaps, another Labour candidate. But I have given a reason why the Independents were not elected-it is simple enough: because they were a lot of dissociated groups; none of them had sufficient backing among the people of Winnipeg to entitle them to represent the people of Winnipeg. The Conservatives had sufficient backing; they had that whole group of 13.7 per cent. Had anyone known the total number of Conservative, Liberal and Labour votes and endeavoured to give to each group the representation to which it was intitled, he could not have done it more fairly than was the case as the result of this election by proportional representation. It is true that there were less votes per member for Conservatives than in the case of any other group and considerably more votes per member for Labour than for any other. Had they elected, say, one more Labour candidate and one less Conservative, the inequality would have been very much greater. As it is at present, you have about one Labour representative for a little over ten per cent of the vote and one Conservative representative for a little less than seven per cent of the vote. Had you changed that, had there been one more Labour member and one less Conservative member, the disparity would be still greater. Labour would have one representative for a little over eight per cent, and the Conservatives would have one for thirteen and a half or nearly fourteen per cent. So you see a fairer result could not have been obtained amongst the parties.
We come to the other question of transferable votes in single constituencies, and there is little enlightenment to be thrown on that by the Manitoba situation. In Manitoba no provision was made in the provincial election for transferable votes in single constituencies. As is liable to be the case in Canada for some time at least,

there were more than the two old groups; there were additional groups. I have from the Canadian Nation figures given of the results in spme of those constituencies, which figures show that many of the elected representatives were minority candidates. It is not, however, fair to say of those men that they were not entitled to their seats, because they obtained the seats under the plan that was established, the only plan on which they could be candidates. No blame, therefore, attaches to them; the blame is on the system. In Brandon, the Labour candidate secured election by 2,007 votes, while 2,648 votes were cast against him for the two nonLabour candidates, so that he was a minority candidate. In the electoral division of Emerson 989 votes elected a Farmer representative, while 1,681 Liberal and Conservative votes were ineffective. In Manitou constituency 1,085 votes elected a Conservative candidate, while 1,927 votes for Liberal and Farmer candidates were wasted, or nearly double the number. In Rock-wood the elected candidate obtained 978 votes, rendering ineffective the 977 votes, or one vote less, for another candidate, and 638 votes for a third candidate. That is, the elected candidate received only 978 votes, while 1,615 votes were cast against him. As I have said, there is no fault attaching to the candidates in that case; they obtained their election under the only system which was available.
We have at present in this House three members elected from constituencies in Ontario against whom the taunt is sometimes hurled that they are minority representatives. The fact that they are minority representatives is not any fault of theirs; it is the fault of the people generally and the fault of this House and of our plan of election. They offered themselves as candidates under the only system available, and they were duly elected under that system. It is very unfair to them that any one should be in a position to claim that they are minority representatives. If we wish to avoid the possibility or even probability of minority representatives in this House, we must adopt the principle of allowing the elector more than one choice, that is, where there is more than one candidate. It is quite plain that, for some time at least, we shall, in our politics, be divided into groups, and we should make our electoral machinery suit changed conditions. There is very little doubt that in the next election three-cornered and even four and five-cornered fights in single constituencies will take place, and it is our duty
['Mr. Thomson.] _
before the next election to provide legislation which will properly meet changed conditions and enable the electors to have complete say as to who shall represent them.
We hear the complaint made by leaders of the present Opposition that the opponents of the Government will be divided and will be fighting against one another in such a way as to weaken the effect of anything they decide to do. On the other hand we hear complaints from leaders and supporters on the Government side that there is danger of unfair understandings and arrangements amongst the leaders of the Opposition groups, and that this will militate against the Government. The way to overcome these dangers, if such exist, is to adopt the principle under discussion, where every elector can exercise his choice to the full limit.
Something has been said by the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sex-smith) with regard to the action of the farmers in forming an organization of their own. I do not think he was quite consistent with what he said before that; I think he rather contradicted himself. Let me, however, say this to my hon. friend, that I think he must admit that he has never seen in this group anything that would justify him in supposing that we want to make this group exclusive. The farmers generally do -not want to form an exclusive political organization; they do not want to be exclusive; they do not want any class to rule. In fact, the main reason of their organization is their objection to class rule. We have had class rule in Canada since Confederation, and we want to do away with that. We have a platform on which we believe that members of every class can stand, that every honest man who wants fair play can stand. Therefore, we stick to that platform. Perhaps I am getting a little out of order; but if so I am only following my hon. friend who spoke before, who was also out of order. We ask for proportional representation amongst other things, so that my hon. friend is with us there.
Personally, I would like to see our law so framed that every opportunity will be given to the electors to decide who shall be their representatives. I realize that the leading issue in the next election campaign will be the issue between a customs tariff, probably somewhat resembling the tariff we have at present, on the one side, and a very low tariff on the other. I need not say where I stand on that question. Still, if the maiority of the people of Canada desire

to retain a protective tariff such as we have at present, or even a higher tariff, they have an absolute right to such a tariff, and notwithstanding my own preference, I wish them to have it. They have the right to rule, and they have the right to decide what should be done. I may believe their course a mistaken one, hut I must grant them the right to make their own mistakes.
I trust this resolution will be adopted by an overwhelming majority of the members of the House, and that it will be followed by immediate and effectual legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I did not arrive in the chamber in time to hear the opening sentences of the speech of the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith); but I think I was in time to hear the greater part of his speech, and I may frankly say that I was very much impressed with many of the arguments which he presented. I have had the privilege of sitting in this House with the hon. member for East Peterborough for a number of years. I know he never advocates anything unless he is absolutely sincere, and he is always very careful in his accumulation of facts and always logical in his presentation of them. I find myself, however, in this position in regard to the resolution before us. Very frankly I confess that I have not given this subject the careful study which has undoubtedly been given to it by the hon. member for East Peterborough and by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson). I find myself then in a position of being ill-informed as to, perhaps, the benefits of this proposed system over our present system. It may he, as these hon. gentlemen urge, that the system of proportional representation, such as is proposed in this resolution, would he vastly superior to the system which has prevailed ever since Confederation, and I am conscious of many defects in that system. I am not sure at the present moment that the system suggested would be better than our present system, with all its difficulties, and that brings me to the objection which I find in the resolution as proposed. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, in order to give each voter an equal share in the representation, some system of proportional representation should he adopted-
Let me stop there. Now if I vote for this resolution, then perforce I am voting in favour of adopting some system of proportional representation, and speaking for myself alone, I have not sufficient information at the present time to convince me
that such a system would be superior to our present system. It is true that the resolution goes on to suggest that a special committee be appointed to gather information in regard to proportional representation with a view to reporting to the House, but I would feel I was in a much better position to cast a vote in regard to proportional representation if I was provided with the information which this committee is supposed to gather than I am now, when the information has not been gathered and presented.
If that part of the resolution were eliminated which asks me to vote in favour of a system of proportional representation, and the resolution merely asked me to support the appointment of a connhittee which was to gather information in regard to proportional representation, I would freely vote for it.
I shall not take up time discussing the subject further, for the reasons I have already given. I do not feel competent to discuss the subject on its merits. I have [DOT] not given it careful study, and I think it is of sufficient importance to warrant hon. members of this House giving it careful consideration. I should like to hear the opinions of hon. gentlemen who have been longer in public life than I have. I should be very glad, indeed, to hear the well-considered opinion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), for instance. He has been a long time in public life and no doubt has given the subject some consideration; whether or not he has gone deeply into the question it is for him to say. Frankly, Sir, I feel that I am not qualified to discuss this matter on its merits. I also feel that I have not sufficient knowledge of the system of proportional representation to enable me to vote for a resolution declaring in favour of it.

The outstanding fact to my mind with regard to proportional representation is that it is here now. It is here in this House. It is in the Ontario Legislature, it is in the Manitoba Legislature, and in British Columbia. Proportional representation is in every place where they have held an election in recent years. The people of Canada are not satisfied with the old system, and they have split themselves into groups, not as the result of proportional representation, however; and if groups we must have, for Heaven's sake let us have intelligent groups. Perhaps the most useful contribution that I can make

to the debate, coming from Manitoba, where the question is no longer an academic one, but where the system has actually been tried, will be to give a few facts with regard to the. trial that was made of the system there during the last election. In the first place, it was tried in Winnipeg alone, and with this extraordinary result, that in Winnipeg we have a group of three parties only, Labour, Liberal and Conservative, whereas in the outlying parts of the province where the old system was in force, we have a group of five, Liberal, Farmer, Conservative, Labour and Independent. It will no doubt be interesting to the House to ascertain how this occurred. I have some figures here which I shall not read at length, but which with the permission of the House I shall place on Hansard, after quoting briefly from them. I have here the actual returns of every constituency in Manitoba, the number of votes polled, the number of candidates, and the results. In Brandon, for instance, where my old friend, General Kirkcaldy was running as a Conservative, he polled 1,245 votes. My old friend, Mr. Clements, a Liberal, polled 1,403 votes, and Albert E. Smith, the Labour man, polled 2,207 votes. This is a fair sample of a modern election where more than two candidates are running. It happens to-day, Mr. Speaker, quite often, I think, that we not only do not have majority representatives, but we have minority ones and this is a fair case in point. In Emerson constituency, the farmers elected a member with a vote of 989. The Government polled 756, and the Conservatives, 925. The man who was elected with 989 votes had against him 1,600 votes of people who did not believe in his policies. It has sometimes been said that if it had not been for proportional representation there would not have been so many groups in the Manitoba House. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read a letter from the Executive Council in Winnipeg.
I am in receipt o your letter of the 23rd ult., with respect to the recent Manitoba elections and I am enclosing herewith the list of the candidates and the votes polled for each in each' constituency In the Province of Manitoba.
I cannot understand how the newspapers are possessed with the idea that proportional representation is responsible for the reduced majority of the Norris Government, as the vote in Winnipeg did not show this by any means. I have given as near as possible the party affiliations of each candidate, but until the House meets it is difficult to accurately state how some of these will line up.
Had proportional representation been in force throughout the whole of the province there is 
no question in the world but that the Norris Government would have received a much larger representation.
One point I want hon. members to realize, is that we are not having groups because of proportional representation, but in spite of it. I think most of the ground has been covered in this debate. A point, however, that presents some difficulty is: What are you going to do in single-member constituencies? Most men feel that it is impossible to group the outside constituencies, and frankly I am of that opinion. Our areas are too far-flung to do it. As a result of the election in Manitoba there is a Bill before the Manitoba House at the present time, and it has passed its second reading, for the purpose of carrying out the idea of the single transferable vote in every constituency in Manitoba. This does not mean group constituencies, but if there are more than three candidates the elector will be given a first, second, and third preference. For instance, if there are three men, one a Conservative, one a Liberal, and one a Farmer, I, being a Liberal, would probably vote for the Liberal. Now, the majority is the majority of the votes cast at the election. Supposing 14,000 votes are cast; half of that would be 7,000, and one over that would be the quota required to elect a member. Now, I vote for the Liberal, and if he has sufficient votes in the first round to elect him, that settles it. If not, it is proposed to drop out the low man and transfer his votes, according to the preference of the votes. Probably, in the next case, I would transfer my vote to the Farmer if my first choice was not elected. These votes are transferred in accordance with the expressed desire of the voter; so that, as a matter of fact, no vote is lost, and it is impossible to have a minority candidate returned. The man who does come back must have at least a majority of one.
I was very much interested the other day, when the debate on patronage was before the House, to hear the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Edwards), suggest that the patronage should be given to the sitting member. I wonder what he would do in a case like Emerson, where the sitting member represented 900, although approximately 1,680 people had voted against him. It is entirely possible under our present system that we may have a House, after the next election, unless there is a change, representing about one-third of the people of Canada. That is quite possible. To-day, this proposal is right in

line with practical politics. It is no longer a matter of academic debate, and I do sincerely trust that the Government will appoint this committee. I agree with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that if the mover of the resolution could recommend the appointment of a committee without committing us to some definite form of proportional representation, it would he very much better. I will vote for it in any case, because it is a right thing; but if this suggestion were adopted I think it would be in the better interests of all concerned. With regard to the figures which I have, with the permission of the House, Mr. Speaker, I would place them on Hansard. The statement gives the names, the number of votes and the number of candidates in every constituency. In some constituencies there were as many as five candidates running. I think that this table would be of general interest to members of the House, and it would be well to have it on Hansard.

I think the hon. member would be better advised to read the list:	It is only in rare and exceptional
cases that documents are permitted to be embodied in Hansard without having been read, and I have never known instances in which this was done in a debate on private member's day. While I regret that this is so, nevertheless it is the fact, and I think it would be well, in the interests of proper procedure, for the hon. member to conform to the rule and read the list.

May I rise to a point of order, Mr. Speaker? If this is a very long statement the reading of it may take up considerable time. This is an extremely important debate, and while the statement may not strike hon. members on its reading, yet in printed form the facts would catch
the eye, and I have no doubt that they would be of interest. I suggest, Sir, that it would be helpful to a proper consideration of the subject if the document were allowed to be placed on Hansard.
